EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Holcombe Road Wildfire started April 19 around 3:00 pm in Crockett County and eventually spread into Val Verde County. The fire started in the wake of a cold front that brought dry air and gusty winds. At the time of ignition, the relative humidity at Del Rio had fallen to 10% and 30 foot winds were from the WNW at 15 to 20 mph with gusts up to 36 mph. The fire burned until May 2 and consumed 25,958 acres. Seven structures, four recreational vehicles, and four outbuildings were destroyed. Thirty-five homes were threatened by the fire and saved.

The fire burned until May 2 and consumed 25,958 acres. Seven structures, four recreational vehicles, and four outbuildings were destroyed. Thirty-five homes were threatened by the fire and saved.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough diving southeast across Eastern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas in the northwest flow aloft during the evening through the early morning hours of May 7th-8th, enhanced large scale forcing ahead of an attendant cold front, resulting in a complex of showers and thunderstorms to develop near and ahead of the front. This mesoscale convective system, or MCS, quickly shifted southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the early morning hours of May 8th, strengthening as it encountered greater instability and a strong southerly low level jet. This resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms containing damaging winds, triggering numerous reports of wind damage across these areas. In addition, strong surface winds with gusts up to 50 mph ahead of the complex of showers and thunderstorms also downed several trees given the wet antecedent soil moisture conditions in place from above normal rainfall observed since the start of the year. These storms exited Northeast Texas prior to daybreak on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell onto a home on East Hiram Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slight severe risk was draped across much of the CWA due to a surface convergent boundary over western counties with an approaching cold front from the north. Supercell thunderstorms developed along the convergent boundary during the late afternoon before forming into a complex line of storms along the front that lasted into the overnight hours. There was ample instability with CAPE over 2000J/kg coupled with decent shear up to 30KT and moisture influx due to the more saturated and unstable southeast low level flow. Early on with the supercells, funnel clouds and large hail were the main threats. Once the line developed and pushed south and east, damaging winds and hail became the hazards with many reports that verified a number of the warnings that were issued.

Based on the damage, wind gusts were estimated at 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed very late this afternoon and early evening as a hot and humid airmass remained in place across eastern Kentucky. The hardest hit area by heavy rainfall was along the Hal Rogers Parkway and Highway 80 corridor, stretching from Leslie County to Floyd County.||A portion of Leslie County saw chunks of a roadway washed away, while parts of Perry and Floyd Counties had motorists stranded and rescued by first responders. Residences near Fisty in Knott County were inundated by quickly rising flood waters.||Localized damage occurred in Harlan County near Molus as thunderstorm winds downed 10-15 large trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and unstable atmosphere developed on the 13th ahead of an approaching upper level short wave. Virga showers had developed out ahead of this upper level feature during the morning and early afternoon. This caused a severe wind gust to 65 mph from a heat burst at the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Graham (Garza County). When thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon, the initial activity was somewhat disorganized. But these initial storms were intense enough to produce pockets of hail as large as ping pong ball size. Eventually the scattered thunderstorms amalgamated into a line and accelerated eastward through the Rolling Plains and into western North Texas during the late evening hours. Several reports of small hail, strong to severe wind gusts and very heavy rainfall were received as the line moved through.

The winds finally decreased by the morning of May 2, but several stations in the Kern County Mountains and Deserts reported gusts above 45 mph through the evening of May 2.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bird Springs Pass RAWS measured a peak wind gust of 63 mph.

The main impact of the frost was on horticulture and fruit crops.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of slow-moving thunderstorms tracked along and just north of a warm front draped along the I-64 corridor during the afternoon and evening of May 16th.  The storms dropped 3 to 4 inches of rain across the southern sections of Scott, Morgan, and Sangamon counties...including 3.84 just southeast of Curran in Sangamon County and 3.05 in Murrayville in Morgan County.  The heavy rainfall created flash flooding of numerous county roads and city viaducts.  In addition, one thunderstorm cell produced dime-sized hail in Franklin in Morgan County.

Thunderstorms producing copious amounts of rainfall impacted the southern sections of Morgan and Sangamon counties during the afternoon of May 16th.  While these storms pushed further east and only scattered lighter showers persisted, many area creeks and streams continued to rise through the evening of May 16th into the morning of May 17th.  As a result, widespread areal flooding occurred from near Murrayville in Morgan County eastward to Chatham and Auburn in Sangamon County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread flooding occurred on area roads from the Scott-Morgan County line west of Murrayville eastward to Franklin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A lone supercell thunderstorm erupted late Thursday afternoon southwest of Memphis (Hall County) and tracked steadily eastward across northern Childress County. While doing so, it shed another storm that moved northeastward into southwest Oklahoma. Very strong instability and moderate wind shear allowed the storms to quickly become severe and start rotating in the middle levels of the atmosphere. The result was that the storms generated giant hail to 3.25 inches in diameter and brief heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hailstorm that began in northeastern Hall County continued to track east-southeast across far northern Childress County, with hailstones larger than teacups at times. However, the majority of the severe hail reports were generally tennis ball size or smaller. No damage information was available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Upper-level troughing remained prominent across the Gulf of Mexico with a speed max extending east-northeast from the Bay of Campeche into the northwest Caribbean Sea. A decaying Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) was lifting north through the Atlantic waters while surface troughing extended from the southern Florida Peninsula southwest into the southern Gulf of Mexico. Given the diffluent pattern aloft, subtle vorticity perturbations, the remnant MCV, and the surface trough, plentiful sources for lift were evident across South Florida that allowed for the development of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms. Additionally, plenty of moisture was distributed areawide with rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour. Abundant moisture along with preceding heavy rainfall and antecedent conditions led to widespread flooding across Miami-Dade and Broward counties. Furthermore, increasing low-level shear behind the MCV whipped up a brief tornado in Miami-Dade County and a funnel cloud in Broward County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS storm survey team found damage consistent with an EF-1 tornado that developed around the Miami Everglades RV Resort and moved discontinuously northwest to near SW 197th Avenue and SW 156th Street. Several campers were tipped over at the Miami Everglades RV Resort, consistent with stronger winds around 90 mph per radar-based statistical model. The majority of the remaining damage was limited to trees and fencing starting east of Krome Avenue around SW 192nd Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dynamic storm system brought severe thunderstorms to a large part of Central Alabama on January 11th.  Deep southerly flow brought rich Gulf moisture northward into Alabama. Anomalously high surface temperatures and moisture content was present in the developing warm sector ahead of the storm system. A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front and moved into west central Alabama late in the morning. The line of storms quickly moved through Central Alabama and exited southeastern areas around sunset.||Although not every location experienced severe weather, widespread wind gusts of 40 to 60 mph were observed along the QLCS. Trees were snapped off or uprooted in numerous locations. Many homes, automobiles, and outbuildings were damaged or destroyed. Several locations likely received straight-line wind gusts of 75 to 80 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees uprooted along Camelia Drive in the city of Prattville.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: National Weather Service meteorologists surveyed damage through the town of Mason on May 28, 2020, from a thunderstorm that took place during the evening of May 27, 2020.  Evidence was found of a narrow corridor of damaging straight-line winds which started just northwest of the town of Mason, and continued as the storm pushed southeast through the city for about 15-20 minutes. Speeds were estimated at 70 to 80 mph, with peak gusts of 85 to 90 mph. These winds snapped large limbs off of several trees and uprooted a few others. A few tin roofs on older homes and businesses were also partially pealed back.  In addition, windows in the city jail were broken, which was likely due to the combination of severe winds and quarter-sized hail.  Special thanks to the county judge for his assistance with this damage survey.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving shortwave trough of low pressure moved through the northern Sierra from late on the 3rd through the morning hours of the 4th bringing with it gusty winds. Ridge gusts topped 87 mph while some wind prone areas along US Highway 395 in Mono County peaked at 50 to 57 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough diving southeast across Eastern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas in the northwest flow aloft during the evening through the early morning hours of May 7th-8th, enhanced large scale forcing ahead of an attendant cold front, resulting in a complex of showers and thunderstorms to develop near and ahead of the front. This mesoscale convective system, or MCS, quickly shifted southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the early morning hours of May 8th, strengthening as it encountered greater instability and a strong southerly low level jet. This resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms containing damaging winds, triggering numerous reports of wind damage across these areas. In addition, strong surface winds with gusts up to 50 mph ahead of the complex of showers and thunderstorms also downed several trees given the wet antecedent soil moisture conditions in place from above normal rainfall observed since the start of the year. These storms exited Northeast Texas prior to daybreak on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed on FM 1519, CR 4321, and CR 1110.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of May 24th, as an upper level disturbance rotated north across East-Central Texas, ahead of a large upper level trough of low pressure slowly drifting east over much of the Rockies. Moderate instability developed during the afternoon is response to diurnal heating and a very moist air mass in place, such that some of these storms became severe, producing hail and multiple reports of damaging winds which downed trees and power lines across East Texas, Northwest Louisiana, and Southeast Oklahoma. These storms eventually weakened by early evening as the air mass stabilized in response to the more widespread rain cooled air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down on County Road 1218.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slight severe risk was draped across much of the CWA due to a surface convergent boundary over western counties with an approaching cold front from the north. Supercell thunderstorms developed along the convergent boundary during the late afternoon before forming into a complex line of storms along the front that lasted into the overnight hours. There was ample instability with CAPE over 2000J/kg coupled with decent shear up to 30KT and moisture influx due to the more saturated and unstable southeast low level flow. Early on with the supercells, funnel clouds and large hail were the main threats. Once the line developed and pushed south and east, damaging winds and hail became the hazards with many reports that verified a number of the warnings that were issued.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong and gusty northerly winds impacted the mountains of Santa Barbara, Ventura and Los Angeles counties. Wind gusts up to around 75 MPH were reported in some areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and unstable atmosphere developed on the 13th ahead of an approaching upper level short wave. Virga showers had developed out ahead of this upper level feature during the morning and early afternoon. This caused a severe wind gust to 65 mph from a heat burst at the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Graham (Garza County). When thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon, the initial activity was somewhat disorganized. But these initial storms were intense enough to produce pockets of hail as large as ping pong ball size. Eventually the scattered thunderstorms amalgamated into a line and accelerated eastward through the Rolling Plains and into western North Texas during the late evening hours. Several reports of small hail, strong to severe wind gusts and very heavy rainfall were received as the line moved through.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A report of quarter size hail was received about two miles northwest of Smyer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread frost occurred over western Kentucky except the extreme western counties bordering the Mississippi River. A strong high pressure system was centered over the Ozark Mountains early on the 9th, resulting in clear skies and chilly northwest winds. The winds were light enough for a brief period of frost in most places. Low temperatures were in the lower to mid 30's. The main impact of the frost was on horticulture and fruit crops.

A tropical disturbance over the South Florida Atlantic waters of Broward and Miami-Dade counties was forecast by NHC to continue moving northeastward into the Western Atlantic waters. NHC showed a 70 percent chance of development into a tropical system in the next 48 hours, mainly in the Northwest Bahamas or the Western Atlantic waters. As the disturbance moved northeastward, deeper moisture worked into the region from the south leading to the continuation of numerous showers and thunderstorms over eastern areas. As this convection progressed towards the east coast metro areas, strong wind gusts along with heavy rainfall and repeated rounds of convection lead to widespread flooding and standing water that lasted into the overnight hours of May 15 into May 16, well after precipitation ended.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An off-duty NWS Employee reported extensive street flooding due to heavy rainfall in areas of Broward County, specifically Pompano Beach area. Water several inches deep and flowing near the intersection of Atlantic Blvd and US-1, the intersection of 15th St and North Andrews Ave, the intersection of 13th St and North Andrews Ave, and the intersection of North Andrews Ave and Copans Rd was reported. Some roadways/intersections were impassable. Multiple pictures received showing the excessive water.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported flooded roadways due to heavy rainfall in the Miami Springs area via Snapmap. Rainfall estimates in the area were 2 to 3 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving upper low pressure system over Southern Oklahoma and Northeast Texas drifted east along the Red River Valley during the afternoon and evening hours of May 26th. This system contributed to a decayed complex of showers and thunderstorms that moved through portions of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning hours, thus stabilizing the air mass through much of the day. However, diurnal heating did contribute to the development of some instability during the late afternoon through the evening hours from Southeast Texas north into portions of East Texas and Northwest Louisiana, as another spoke of upper level energy rotated north-northeast around the center of the upper level low pressure area. This resulted in scattered shower and thunderstorm development by late afternoon through much of the evening hours, with some of these storms becoming severe, resulting in several reports of large hail. These storms persisted into the early morning hours of May 27th, but weakened given the loss of instability.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell and damaged a Texas DPS patrol vehicle and caused an accident on I-20 near Marshall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving upper level low pressure system drifted east across Central and Eastern Texas during the daytime hours of May 16th. Meanwhile, the attendant surface low pressure system over East Central Texas drifted east into Northeast Texas during the afternoon, with a southerly low level jet allowing for a warm front to mix north into East Texas, extreme Northern Louisiana, into Southern Arkansas through the evening. Although daytime heating was limited due to extensive cloud cover and periods of showers, large scale forcing and adequate low level wind shear contributed to the development of numerous low-topped supercell showers and a few thunderstorms, several of which spawned tornadoes and wall clouds across portions of extreme Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Southeast Oklahoma throughout the afternoon and evening. As drier air began to entrain ahead of this upper low pressure system, and the warm front had shifted north into the northern sections of Southwest Arkansas by mid-evening, the tornado threat subsided considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A KTEN TV viewer captured a picture of a funnel cloud over Idabel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of May 24th, as an upper level disturbance rotated north across East-Central Texas, ahead of a large upper level trough of low pressure slowly drifting east over much of the Rockies. Moderate instability developed during the afternoon is response to diurnal heating and a very moist air mass in place, such that some of these storms became severe, producing hail and multiple reports of damaging winds which downed trees and power lines across East Texas, Northwest Louisiana, and Southeast Oklahoma. These storms eventually weakened by early evening as the air mass stabilized in response to the more widespread rain cooled air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown onto power lines on County Road 1127.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slight severe risk was draped across much of the CWA due to a surface convergent boundary over western counties with an approaching cold front from the north. Supercell thunderstorms developed along the convergent boundary during the late afternoon before forming into a complex line of storms along the front that lasted into the overnight hours. There was ample instability with CAPE over 2000J/kg coupled with decent shear up to 30KT and moisture influx due to the more saturated and unstable southeast low level flow. Early on with the supercells, funnel clouds and large hail were the main threats. Once the line developed and pushed south and east, damaging winds and hail became the hazards with many reports that verified a number of the warnings that were issued.

A shortwave trough diving southeast across Eastern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas in the northwest flow aloft during the evening through the early morning hours of May 7th-8th, enhanced large scale forcing ahead of an attendant cold front, resulting in a complex of showers and thunderstorms to develop near and ahead of the front. This mesoscale convective system, or MCS, quickly shifted southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the early morning hours of May 8th, strengthening as it encountered greater instability and a strong southerly low level jet. This resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms containing damaging winds, triggering numerous reports of wind damage across these areas. In addition, strong surface winds with gusts up to 50 mph ahead of the complex of showers and thunderstorms also downed several trees given the wet antecedent soil moisture conditions in place from above normal rainfall observed since the start of the year. These storms exited North Louisiana shortly after daybreak on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down onto Highway 160 near the Claiborne Parish line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and unstable atmosphere developed on the 13th ahead of an approaching upper level short wave. Virga showers had developed out ahead of this upper level feature during the morning and early afternoon. This caused a severe wind gust to 65 mph from a heat burst at the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Graham (Garza County). When thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon, the initial activity was somewhat disorganized. But these initial storms were intense enough to produce pockets of hail as large as ping pong ball size. Eventually the scattered thunderstorms amalgamated into a line and accelerated eastward through the Rolling Plains and into western North Texas during the late evening hours. Several reports of small hail, strong to severe wind gusts and very heavy rainfall were received as the line moved through.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail was measured by a member of the public about three miles north of Abernathy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of high pressure built into California on May 25 and May 26. This resulted in much above normal daytime temperatures on both days with some locations setting new daily records on May 26. The high then strengthened on May 27 and May 28 resulting in widespread record heat over the region on both days with highs in the San Joaquin Valley mainly between 103 and 107 on both days. Triple digit heat was also observed across portions of the Sierra foothills and Kern County Deserts. Temperatures cooled by several degrees on May 29 and lowered to below seasonal averages by May 30 as the large area high pressure broke down, and a cold front pushed through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime highs ranged between 100 and 104 degrees on May 26 and between 103 and 107 degrees on May 27 and May 28.

A tropical disturbance in the Florida Straits was forecast by NHC to move northeastward into the Atlantic waters of South Florida before continuing to move northeastward into the Western Atlantic waters. NHC showed a 70 percent chance of development into a tropical system in the next 48 hours, mainly in the Northwest Bahamas or the Western Atlantic waters. As the disturbance moved northeastward, deeper moisture worked into the region from the south leading to numerous showers and thunderstorms over eastern areas. As this convection progressed towards the east coast metro areas, especially Broward and Miami-Dade counties, heavy rainfall and repeated rounds of convection lead to widespread flooding and standing water that lasted into the overnight hours of May 15 into May 16, well after precipitation ended.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An off-duty NWS Meteorologist reported significant street. flooding several inches deep at the intersection of NW 47th Ave and NW 21st St, and vicinity, in Lauderhill, FL. Flood waters accumulated with heavy rains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A sharp upper level trough diving and developing through the nation's midsection drove a strong, but dry, cold front deep into Mexico on February 26th.  Strong high pressure followed quickly behind the front overnight, and the combination of very dry and chilly air with nearly calm winds set the stage for a minor freeze around sunrise on the 27th.  The freeze exacerbated drought conditions across the region and maintained the threat of wildfire growth into early March as fuels remained highly cured.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A collection of observations between Encino and Falfurrias indicated a freeze, likely with frost in some locations. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving upper level low pressure system drifted east across Central and Eastern Texas during the daytime hours of May 16th. Meanwhile, the attendant surface low pressure system over East Central Texas drifted east into Northeast Texas during the afternoon, with a southerly low level jet allowing for a warm front to mix north into East Texas, extreme Northern Louisiana, into Southern Arkansas through the evening. Although daytime heating was limited due to extensive cloud cover and periods of showers, large scale forcing and adequate low level wind shear contributed to the development of numerous low-topped supercell showers and a few thunderstorms, several of which spawned tornadoes and wall clouds across portions of extreme Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Southeast Oklahoma throughout the afternoon and evening. As drier air began to entrain ahead of this upper low pressure system, and the warm front had shifted north into the northern sections of Southwest Arkansas by mid-evening, the tornado threat subsided considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Many roads were impassable due to flooding throughout the city of Idabel.

A slight severe risk was draped across much of the CWA due to a surface convergent boundary over western counties with an approaching cold front from the north. Supercell thunderstorms developed along the convergent boundary during the late afternoon before forming into a complex line of storms along the front that lasted into the overnight hours. There was ample instability with CAPE over 2000J/kg coupled with decent shear up to 30KT and moisture influx due to the more saturated and unstable southeast low level flow. Early on with the supercells, funnel clouds and large hail were the main threats. Once the line developed and pushed south and east, damaging winds and hail became the hazards with many reports that verified a number of the warnings that were issued.

A slow moving low pressure system drifted across the Ohio Valley on May 18 and 19, bringing several rounds of heavy rain to the eastern reaches of the Commonwealth. The hardest hit areas spanned from the Cumberland Valley to the Bluegrass region where widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6 inches fell over the two day period. This caused several road closures and flooding of low lying areas as points on the Red, Kentucky, and Cumberland Rivers reached minor to moderate flood stage. In Jackson County, a couple of water rescues had to be performed as motorists became trapped.||Flash flooding was confined to the afternoon and evening hours of May 18th across portions of Pulaski and Fleming Counties, while isolated severe thunderstorm winds occurred in Laurel and Jackson Counties. Additionally, a home near Somerset was hit by lightning while mudslides occurred near Bledsoe in Harlan County on U.S. Highway 421, on Kentucky Highway 1110 south of Jackson in Breathitt County, and on Proctor Road near Beattyville in Lee County due to the abundant rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter observed water of 4 to 6 inches deep flowing over the intersection of Slate Branch Road and Oak Hill Road southwest of Somerset.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough diving southeast across Eastern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas in the northwest flow aloft during the evening through the early morning hours of May 7th-8th, enhanced large scale forcing ahead of an attendant cold front, resulting in a complex of showers and thunderstorms to develop near and ahead of the front. This mesoscale convective system, or MCS, quickly shifted southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the early morning hours of May 8th, strengthening as it encountered greater instability and a strong southerly low level jet. This resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms containing damaging winds, triggering numerous reports of wind damage across these areas. In addition, strong surface winds with gusts up to 50 mph ahead of the complex of showers and thunderstorms also downed several trees given the wet antecedent soil moisture conditions in place from above normal rainfall observed since the start of the year. These storms exited North Louisiana shortly after daybreak on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A picture was posted to social media of large limbs that were downed in the Shady Grove neighborhood in Bossier City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving upper level low pressure system drifted east across Central and Eastern Texas during the daytime hours of May 16th. Meanwhile, the attendant surface low pressure system over East Central Texas drifted east into Northeast Texas during the afternoon, with a southerly low level jet allowing for a warm front to mix north into East Texas, extreme Northern Louisiana, into Southern Arkansas through the evening. Although daytime heating was limited due to extensive cloud cover and periods of showers, large scale forcing and adequate low level wind shear contributed to the development of numerous low-topped supercell showers and a few thunderstorms, several of which spawned tornadoes and wall clouds across portions of extreme Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Southeast Oklahoma throughout the afternoon and evening. As drier air began to entrain ahead of this upper low pressure system, and the warm front had shifted north into the northern sections of Southwest Arkansas by mid-evening, the tornado threat subsided considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This is a continuation of the extreme Southwest Little River County, Arkansas tornado. This tornado was documented by multiple witnesses via video and pictures as it moved northwest across an open field in extreme Southeast McCurtain County before lifting. Since the NWS survey team was unable to access this area, an EF rating could not be assigned and thus, this tornado will be rated an EF-Unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and unstable atmosphere developed on the 13th ahead of an approaching upper level short wave. Virga showers had developed out ahead of this upper level feature during the morning and early afternoon. This caused a severe wind gust to 65 mph from a heat burst at the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Graham (Garza County). When thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon, the initial activity was somewhat disorganized. But these initial storms were intense enough to produce pockets of hail as large as ping pong ball size. Eventually the scattered thunderstorms amalgamated into a line and accelerated eastward through the Rolling Plains and into western North Texas during the late evening hours. Several reports of small hail, strong to severe wind gusts and very heavy rainfall were received as the line moved through.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of high pressure built into California on May 25 and May 26. This resulted in much above normal daytime temperatures on both days with some locations setting new daily records on May 26. The high then strengthened on May 27 and May 28 resulting in widespread record heat over the region on both days with highs in the San Joaquin Valley mainly between 103 and 107 on both days. Triple digit heat was also observed across portions of the Sierra foothills and Kern County Deserts. Temperatures cooled by several degrees on May 29 and lowered to below seasonal averages by May 30 as the large area high pressure broke down, and a cold front pushed through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime highs ranged between 100 and 104 degrees on May 26 and between 103 and 107 degrees on May 27 and May 28.

A strong high pressure system was centered over the Ozark Mountains early on the 9th, resulting in clear skies and chilly northwest winds. The winds were light enough for a brief period of frost in most places. Low temperatures were in the lower to mid 30's. The main impact of the frost was on horticulture and fruit crops.

A tropical disturbance in the Florida Straits was forecast by NHC to move northeastward into the Atlantic waters of South Florida before continuing to move northeastward into the Western Atlantic waters. NHC showed a 70 percent chance of development into a tropical system in the next 48 hours, mainly in the Northwest Bahamas or the Western Atlantic waters. As the disturbance moved northeastward, deeper moisture worked into the region from the south leading to numerous showers and thunderstorms over eastern areas. As this convection progressed towards the east coast metro areas, especially Broward and Miami-Dade counties, heavy rainfall and repeated rounds of convection lead to widespread flooding and standing water that lasted into the overnight hours of May 15 into May 16, well after precipitation ended.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of minor flooding in the Plantation area. A trained spotter in Plantation reported 6 inches of standing water on the roadside near Ridgewood Lane. The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) webcam indicated standing water on the roadway at the intersection of Broward Blvd and University Dr, blocking the right driving lane completely.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Arthur, which was moving over the outer banks of North Carolina, was forecast to continue moving northeastward off the Mid-Atlantic coastline. At the same time, the tail of Arthur, basically a trough of low pressure, extended into the southeastern portion of the country. This also combined with a mid to upper level area of low pressure moving into the Tennessee Valley and a trough of low pressure moving into the eastern Gulf of Mexico which allowed for a south southwesterly flow across South Florida. This allowed for the Gulf coast sea breeze to push inland as the east coast sea breeze remained pushed up against the east coast. This eventually lead to the development of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across all of South Florida. The primary impacts with these storms were heavy rainfall and associated flooding, frequent lightning strikes, small hail, and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several inches of rain, with measured amounts ranging from 4 to 8 inches, and locally higher amounts, caused flooding in portions of Boynton and Delray Beach. Broadcast media shared a video that showed flooding near the intersection of Congress Ave and Woolbright Rd in Boynton Beach. One car stalled while others turned around. The Weather Underground station KFLDELRA49 in the Sabal Lakes Community of Delray Beach measured 5.41 inches of rain whereas the Weather Underground station KFLDELRA71 near Lake Ida in Delray Beach measured 7.37 inches of rain.

An area of low pressure that dumped over a foot of rain over portions of the east coast the past few days is now Tropical Storm Bertha, which made landfall along the South Carolina coast. A series of weak upper-level impulses also slid across South Florida throughout the course of the day. Consequently, wind flow (and the steering flow) continued to have a slight southwesterly component which pushed showers and thunderstorms towards the east coast. Some drying aloft and cooling 500 mb temps allowed for some steeping of mid-level lapse rates. Plentiful low-level moisture was also still available with PWATs close to 1.6 inches. This abundance of moisture allowed convection to tap into it, creating widespread showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon hours with high rainfall rates. Unfortunately, this was the area that continued to be the most susceptible to hydrological issues with a continued Flood Watch through 8 PM EDT. Lastly, given sufficient precipitation loading and DCAPE over 1000J/kg, a few stronger wind gusts occurred along with some hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter inch hail was reported with a strong thunderstorm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A sharp upper level trough diving and developing through the nation's midsection drove a strong, but dry, cold front deep into Mexico on February 26th.  Strong high pressure followed quickly behind the front overnight, and the combination of very dry and chilly air with nearly calm winds set the stage for a minor freeze around sunrise on the 27th.  The freeze exacerbated drought conditions across the region and maintained the threat of wildfire growth into early March as fuels remained highly cured.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A collection of mesonet and cooperative observations between Armstrong and Sarita reached freezing temperatures around sunrise on February 27.  Minimum temperatures fell to between 28 and 33, with times estimated through proxy observation at mesonet/remote automated weather station (RAWS) sites. The cooperative site 4 miles southeast of Armstrong recorded a low of 28 degrees at around 7 AM.

Weak Santa Ana winds occurred February 19th through 20th. Rainfall amounts ranged from 0.25 to 1.00 across the region. The coastal slopes locally saw over 1 inch of rainfall. Elevated convection formed along the coast on the evening of the 21st, with lightning observed in Huntington Beach and Encinitas. Another secondary area of heavier showers and thunderstorms impacted Orange and San Diego counties on February 22nd. Pea-sized hail occurred in San Diego and Orange counties. Snow occurred in the mountains, mainly on the evening of the 22nd, where up to 5 inches of snow fell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spotters reported up to 5 inches of snow in Big Bear and Snow Valley. Most of the snow fell overnight on the 22nd into the 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After an unusually wet January, another strong storm system brought more heavy rainfall, flooding, and severe storms to parts of Middle Tennessee on February 5th. These storms spawned 6 weak tornadoes and widespread straight-line wind damage. In addition, heavy rainfall affected much of Middle Tennessee throughout the day, causing significant flooding in many areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous roads were flooded across Maury County, including Tom Lunn Road at Port Royal Road and Kedron Road in Spring Hill. A water rescue was conducted at King Hollow Road and Mt. Joy Road in far southwest Maury County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A bitterly cold airmass spilled into central Illinois behind a departing cold front on February 13th.  High temperatures were initially in the lower 30s shortly after midnight, followed by falling temperatures and increasing winds throughout the day.  Air temperatures eventually bottomed out near zero by the early morning of February 14th, while wind-chill values dipped as low as 10 below to 20 below zero.  Due to the frigid temperatures, a man in Peoria lost his life due to hypothermia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 64-year old homeless man from Peoria died in his car around midday on February 13th.  Temperatures at the time of his death were in the teens while wind-chill values were sub-zero.  An autopsy revealed his cause of death as hypothermia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving upper level low pressure system drifted east across Central and Eastern Texas during the daytime hours of May 16th. Meanwhile, the attendant surface low pressure system over East Central Texas drifted east into Northeast Texas during the afternoon, with a southerly low level jet allowing for a warm front to mix north into East Texas, extreme Northern Louisiana, into Southern Arkansas through the evening. Although daytime heating was limited due to extensive cloud cover and periods of showers, large scale forcing and adequate low level wind shear contributed to the development of numerous low-topped supercell showers and a few thunderstorms, several of which spawned tornadoes and wall clouds across portions of extreme Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Southeast Oklahoma throughout the afternoon and evening. As drier air began to entrain ahead of this upper low pressure system, and the warm front had shifted north into the northern sections of Southwest Arkansas by mid-evening, the tornado threat subsided considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A waterspout was documented by video by a game warden on Lake Wright Patman in extreme Northern Cass County. This waterspout then moved northwest into extreme Southern Bowie County across the lake. This waterspout was rated an EF-Unknown due to the lack of damage indicators on the lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of May 24th, as an upper level disturbance rotated north across East-Central Texas, ahead of a large upper level trough of low pressure slowly drifting east over much of the Rockies. Moderate instability developed during the afternoon is response to diurnal heating and a very moist air mass in place, such that some of these storms became severe, producing hail and multiple reports of damaging winds which downed trees and power lines across East Texas, Northwest Louisiana, and Southeast Oklahoma. These storms eventually weakened by early evening as the air mass stabilized in response to the more widespread rain cooled air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on FM 1000.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slight severe risk was draped across much of the CWA due to a surface convergent boundary over western counties with an approaching cold front from the north. Supercell thunderstorms developed along the convergent boundary during the late afternoon before forming into a complex line of storms along the front that lasted into the overnight hours. There was ample instability with CAPE over 2000J/kg coupled with decent shear up to 30KT and moisture influx due to the more saturated and unstable southeast low level flow. Early on with the supercells, funnel clouds and large hail were the main threats. Once the line developed and pushed south and east, damaging winds and hail became the hazards with many reports that verified a number of the warnings that were issued.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving low pressure system drifted across the Ohio Valley on May 18 and 19, bringing several rounds of heavy rain to the eastern reaches of the Commonwealth. The hardest hit areas spanned from the Cumberland Valley to the Bluegrass region where widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6 inches fell over the two day period. This caused several road closures and flooding of low lying areas as points on the Red, Kentucky, and Cumberland Rivers reached minor to moderate flood stage. In Jackson County, a couple of water rescues had to be performed as motorists became trapped.||Flash flooding was confined to the afternoon and evening hours of May 18th across portions of Pulaski and Fleming Counties, while isolated severe thunderstorm winds occurred in Laurel and Jackson Counties. Additionally, a home near Somerset was hit by lightning while mudslides occurred near Bledsoe in Harlan County on U.S. Highway 421, on Kentucky Highway 1110 south of Jackson in Breathitt County, and on Proctor Road near Beattyville in Lee County due to the abundant rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter observed 4 to 6 inches of flowing water over West Bourbon Road on the southwest side of Somerset.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough diving southeast across Eastern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas in the northwest flow aloft during the evening through the early morning hours of May 7th-8th, enhanced large scale forcing ahead of an attendant cold front, resulting in a complex of showers and thunderstorms to develop near and ahead of the front. This mesoscale convective system, or MCS, quickly shifted southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the early morning hours of May 8th, strengthening as it encountered greater instability and a strong southerly low level jet. This resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms containing damaging winds, triggering numerous reports of wind damage across these areas. In addition, strong surface winds with gusts up to 50 mph ahead of the complex of showers and thunderstorms also downed several trees given the wet antecedent soil moisture conditions in place from above normal rainfall observed since the start of the year. These storms exited Northeast Texas prior to daybreak on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong gradient winds downed trees all throughout Rusk County including FM 225, FM 1798, CR 4137, Highway 43 East, FM 95, Highway 315, CR 368 East, CR 4255, FM 2011 and FM 5081.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports of wind damage and an isolated tornado accompanied a squall line of thunderstorms that moved rapidly east-southeast. The wind damage was mainly along and south of a line from Van Buren to Greenville to Sikeston. The atmosphere was moderately unstable, with cape values on the order of 1500 to 2000 J/kg. The relatively compact but organized and vigorous convective system maintained intensity as it progressed east to the Mississippi River. The damaging wind events occurred along and south of a surface frontal boundary, where dew points were in the mid 60's.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Five miles north of Oxly, a trained spotter measured a wind gust to 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated severe thunderstorm occurred within a broken line of showers and weaker storms. This activity occurred within a rather strong southwest wind flow in the warm sector of a low pressure center over far northwest Illinois. The cold front arced from the low into central Illinois and then southwest across south central Missouri. Storm coverage and intensity was tempered by limited instability.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A steeple was blown off a church. A tree was blown onto a home, causing roof damage. Power lines were down and a couple large trees were down across Highway 121.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and unstable atmosphere developed on the 13th ahead of an approaching upper level short wave. Virga showers had developed out ahead of this upper level feature during the morning and early afternoon. This caused a severe wind gust to 65 mph from a heat burst at the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Graham (Garza County). When thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon, the initial activity was somewhat disorganized. But these initial storms were intense enough to produce pockets of hail as large as ping pong ball size. Eventually the scattered thunderstorms amalgamated into a line and accelerated eastward through the Rolling Plains and into western North Texas during the late evening hours. Several reports of small hail, strong to severe wind gusts and very heavy rainfall were received as the line moved through.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Graham measured severe wind gusts from 1910 CST through 1920 CST. The peak wind gust measured was 70 mph.

Although cloud bases were relatively high, no high wind reports were observed with only hail up to the size of golf balls. After thunderstorms had moved into the Rolling Plains by late evening, stratiform precipitation developed over the eastern South Plains. This stratiform precipitation caused a wind gust to 63 mph from a heat burst at a Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Floydada (Floyd County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local broadcast media reported hail up to golf ball size northwest of Shallowater along US Highway 84. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of high pressure built into California on May 25 and May 26. This resulted in much above normal daytime temperatures on both days with some locations setting new daily records on May 26. The high then strengthened on May 27 and May 28 resulting in widespread record heat over the region on both days with highs in the San Joaquin Valley mainly between 103 and 107 on both days. Triple digit heat was also observed across portions of the Sierra foothills and Kern County Deserts. Temperatures cooled by several degrees on May 29 and lowered to below seasonal averages by May 30 as the large area high pressure broke down, and a cold front pushed through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime highs ranged between 100 and 104 degrees on May 26 and between 103 and 107 degrees on May 27 and May 28.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread frost occurred over southern Illinois except the southern tip around Cairo. A strong high pressure system was centered over the Ozark Mountains early on the 9th, resulting in clear skies and chilly northwest winds. The winds were light enough for a brief period of frost in most places. Low temperatures were in the lower to mid 30's. The main impact of the frost was on horticulture and fruit crops.

Tropical Storm Arthur, which was moving over the outer banks of North Carolina, was forecast to continue moving northeastward off the Mid-Atlantic coastline. At the same time, the tail of Arthur, basically a trough of low pressure, extended into the southeastern portion of the country. This also combined with a mid to upper level area of low pressure moving into the Tennessee Valley and a trough of low pressure moving into the eastern Gulf of Mexico which allowed for a south southwesterly flow across South Florida. This allowed for the Gulf coast sea breeze to push inland as the east coast sea breeze remained pushed up against the east coast. This eventually lead to the development of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across all of South Florida. The primary impacts with these storms were heavy rainfall and associated flooding, frequent lightning strikes, small hail, and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported multiple reports of flooding, including streets covered in several inches of water in Miami near NW 3rd Ave and NW 18th Street, due to repeated rounds of showers and thunderstorms.

An upper level shortwave trough moved through West Texas and interacted with a dryline to generate thunderstorms. The airmass was strongly unstable with only modest vertical wind shear and high precipitable water. Storms evolved into a line as they moved across South Central Texas producing large hail, damaging wind gusts, and one tornado. They also produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 80 mph that uprooted trees in Fair Oaks Ranch. This report was from mPING.

Damaging winds occurred with the storms near Cotulla and over portions of the Coastal Bend.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cotulla-La Salle County Airport ASOS measured a gust to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A sharp upper level trough diving and developing through the nation's midsection drove a strong, but dry, cold front deep into Mexico on February 26th.  Strong high pressure followed quickly behind the front overnight, and the combination of very dry and chilly air with nearly calm winds set the stage for a minor freeze around sunrise on the 27th.  The freeze exacerbated drought conditions across the region and maintained the threat of wildfire growth into early March as fuels remained highly cured.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In much of Starr County, based on observations from multiple sites along the Rio Grande and other proxy locations in Zapata, Brooks, and northern Hidalgo County, minimum temperatures fell to between 28 and 32 degrees around sunrise on the 27th. At the cooperative observing station in Rio Grande City, the minimum temperature reached the freezing point right around sunrise.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong influx of moisture, along with a potent upper level jet stream and incoming cold front brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms, some heavy from the early morning of the 5th through the early morning of the 6th.  The first round yielded heavy rainfall in northwest Alabama through southern middle Tennessee during the early morning of the 5th.  A second round occurred with a line of thunderstorms during the late morning and midday hours.  Intense rainfall in a short period of time led to several instances of flash flooding of small creeks and streams.  Several roads were closed or barricaded as a result.||Then, a strong to severe line of thunderstorms developed in Mississippi during the afternoon of the 6th and rolled east through all of north Alabama and southern middle Tennessee during the evening hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Just one week after severe storms brought 6 tornadoes and significant flooding to southern and eastern Middle Tennessee, another storm system spawned another round of severe weather and heavy rainfall in the same areas on February 12th. A line of strong to severe thunderstorms called a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) developed during the afternoon hours across southwest Middle Tennessee and northern Alabama, then moved northeast producing widespread straight-line wind damage and one confirmed tornado in Lawrence County. In addition, heavy rainfall caused more flooding in many parts of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large 11.25 miles long by 1.25 miles wide downburst struck southeastern Lawrence County from the Alabama border northeastward through the Five Points area to the Giles County line. Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in this area, several barns and outbuildings were damaged or destroyed, and a few homes suffered minor roof damage. Winds were estimated up to 75 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread showers and thunderstorms developed over northeastern Oklahoma and southeastern Kansas during the afternoon of the 23rd, to the north of a frontal boundary, and with the approach of an upper level disturbance. Moderate to locally heavy rainfall continued across this region through the morning of the 24th. Widespread rainfall amounts of one to three inches occurred over far northeastern Oklahoma and southeastern Kansas, resulting in moderate flooding of the Neosho River near Commerce.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Neosho River near Commerce rose above its flood stage of 15 feet at 10:45 pm CST on February 24th. The river crested at 18.71 feet at 12:15 pm CST on the 26th, resulting in moderate flooding. Low lying areas around Miami were flooded, including Riverview Park, and Highway 125 near the Fairgrounds was flooded. The river fell below flood stage at 7:15 am CDT on the 28th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After an unusually wet January, another strong storm system brought more heavy rainfall, flooding, and severe storms to parts of Middle Tennessee on February 5th. A line of strong to severe thunderstorms known as a QLCS (Quasi-linear Convective System) developed in northern Mississippi and moved across southern and eastern Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours. These storms spawned 6 weak tornadoes and widespread straight-line wind damage. In addition, heavy rainfall affected much of Middle Tennessee throughout the day, causing significant flooding in many areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This EF-1 tornado initially touched down along Glenn Springs Road downing several trees including a large tree falling on a house. The tornado then crossed Highway 64 continuing its destruction of mostly trees, power lines, and roofs as it moved through the city of Lawrenceburg. Several large trees were snapped or uprooted right in the heart of the city, especially around the public library where one tree fell onto the building and caused significant roof damage. The tornado then moved east-northeast into a more residential neighborhood where additional large trees were uprooted. The tornado weakened as it moved into rural eastern Lawrence County where mostly trees, outbuildings, and a barn were damaged. The tornado lifted just before reaching the Lawrence/Giles County line.

A slow moving upper level low pressure system drifted east across Central and Eastern Texas during the daytime hours of May 16th. Meanwhile, the attendant surface low pressure system over East Central Texas drifted east into Northeast Texas during the afternoon, with a southerly low level jet allowing for a warm front to mix north into East Texas, extreme Northern Louisiana, into Southern Arkansas through the evening. Although daytime heating was limited due to extensive cloud cover and periods of showers, large scale forcing and adequate low level wind shear contributed to the development of numerous low-topped supercell showers and a few thunderstorms, several of which spawned tornadoes and wall clouds across portions of extreme Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Southeast Oklahoma throughout the afternoon and evening. As drier air began to entrain ahead of this upper low pressure system, and the warm front had shifted north into the northern sections of Southwest Arkansas by mid-evening, the tornado threat subsided considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County Road 4321 between Avery and Dekalb was impassable due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of May 24th, as an upper level disturbance rotated north across East-Central Texas, ahead of a large upper level trough of low pressure slowly drifting east over much of the Rockies. Moderate instability developed during the afternoon is response to diurnal heating and a very moist air mass in place, such that some of these storms became severe, producing hail and multiple reports of damaging winds which downed trees and power lines across East Texas, Northwest Louisiana, and Southeast Oklahoma. These storms eventually weakened by early evening as the air mass stabilized in response to the more widespread rain cooled air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and power lines were downed across Red River County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid-upper level low and attendant cold front were approaching the Florida peninsula which allowed for southwesterly surface flow. This consequently would pin the Atlantic sea breeze along the east coast. This along with a weak residual boundary helped with low-level convergence and lift which led to scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern Broward and Miami-Dade counties. Some gusty winds and hail were reported with the strongest activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported penny to dime size hail near a Country Club in Miami Lakes, FL associated with a thunderstorm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Upper-level troughing remained prominent across the Gulf of Mexico with a speed max extending east-northeast from the Bay of Campeche into the northwest Caribbean Sea. A decaying Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) was lifting north through the Atlantic waters while surface troughing extended from the southern Florida Peninsula southwest into the southern Gulf of Mexico. Given the diffluent pattern aloft, subtle vorticity perturbations, the remnant MCV, and the surface trough, plentiful sources for lift were evident across South Florida that allowed for the development of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms. Additionally, plenty of moisture was distributed areawide with rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour. Abundant moisture along with preceding heavy rainfall and antecedent conditions led to widespread flooding across Miami-Dade and Broward counties. Furthermore, increasing low-level shear behind the MCV whipped up a brief tornado in Miami-Dade County and a funnel cloud in Broward County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of flooding via law enforcement, an off-duty NWS employee, and members of the public. City of Miami police reported flooding along and east of Biscayne Blvd from 15th Street to 27th Street. An off-duty NWS employee reported street flooding in Brickell, near Miami Ave and South 9th Street. Social media reports via various members of the public reported flooding in Brickell impeding travel near Brickell Ave and Coral Way. At least one vehicle has been stranded with water appearing to reach halfway up the car wheels and into the car's engine.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: At approximately 1041LST, a 62-year-old man and his wife, both from Orlando, entered the surf at an unguarded beach near the 4600 block of South Atlantic Avenue just north of Ponce Inlet. The couple was quickly overtaken by a rip current and rough surf conditions. A passerby noticed the woman calling for help and called 911. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough diving southeast across Eastern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas in the northwest flow aloft during the evening through the early morning hours of May 7th-8th, enhanced large scale forcing ahead of an attendant cold front, resulting in a complex of showers and thunderstorms to develop near and ahead of the front. This mesoscale convective system, or MCS, quickly shifted southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the early morning hours of May 8th, strengthening as it encountered greater instability and a strong southerly low level jet. This resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms containing damaging winds, triggering numerous reports of wind damage across these areas. In addition, strong surface winds with gusts up to 50 mph ahead of the complex of showers and thunderstorms also downed several trees given the wet antecedent soil moisture conditions in place from above normal rainfall observed since the start of the year. These storms exited Northeast Texas prior to daybreak on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong gradient winds downed trees on Highway 323 about 2 miles east of Highway 42 and also on FM 225 north of Laneville.

CZ_NAME: WESTERN SAN JOAQUIN VALLEY IN KERN COUNTY
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of high pressure built into California on May 25 and May 26. This resulted in much above normal daytime temperatures on both days with some locations setting new daily records on May 26. The high then strengthened on May 27 and May 28 resulting in widespread record heat over the region on both days with highs in the San Joaquin Valley mainly between 103 and 107 on both days. Triple digit heat was also observed across portions of the Sierra foothills and Kern County Deserts. Temperatures cooled by several degrees on May 29 and lowered to below seasonal averages by May 30 as the large area high pressure broke down, and a cold front pushed through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime highs ranged between 100 and 104 degrees on May 26 and between 103 and 107 degrees on May 27 and May 28.

Tropical Storm Arthur, which was moving over the outer banks of North Carolina, was forecast to continue moving northeastward off the Mid-Atlantic coastline. At the same time, the tail of Arthur, basically a trough of low pressure, extended into the southeastern portion of the country. This also combined with a mid to upper level area of low pressure moving into the Tennessee Valley and a trough of low pressure moving into the eastern Gulf of Mexico which allowed for a south southwesterly flow across South Florida. This allowed for the Gulf coast sea breeze to push inland as the east coast sea breeze remained pushed up against the east coast. This eventually lead to the development of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across all of South Florida. The primary impacts with these storms were heavy rainfall and associated flooding, frequent lightning strikes, small hail, and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported heavy rainfall associated with showers and storms in Davie, FL. Home surveillance cameras captured the moment a patio roof collapsed after a deluge of rain. Pieces of furniture were moving all over the patio. Fortunately, no one was injured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface high pressure over the Great Basin brought gusty cold Santa Ana winds to Southern California. Gusty winds occurred mainly on the 3rd and 4th, with peak gusts around 70-75 mph in the wind prone locations (passes, mountains, canyons). The dry air mass brought extreme radiational cooling to the valleys and High Desert each night. Temperatures dipped down into the mid 30s along the coast, the mid 20s to mid 30s for the valleys, and into the teens and low 20s in the High Desert.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Whitewater RAWS reported a peak wind gust of 62 knots between 2200 and 2300 PST on February 2nd.

Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of May 24th, as an upper level disturbance rotated north across East-Central Texas, ahead of a large upper level trough of low pressure slowly drifting east over much of the Rockies. Moderate instability developed during the afternoon is response to diurnal heating and a very moist air mass in place, such that some of these storms became severe, producing hail and multiple reports of damaging winds which downed trees and power lines across East Texas, Northwest Louisiana, and Southeast Oklahoma. These storms eventually weakened by early evening as the air mass stabilized in response to the more widespread rain cooled air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down in the Saint Charles neighborhood in Southeast Shreveport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of May 24th, as an upper level disturbance rotated north across East-Central Texas, ahead of a large upper level trough of low pressure slowly drifting east over much of the Rockies. Moderate instability developed during the afternoon is response to diurnal heating and a very moist air mass in place, such that some of these storms became severe, producing hail and multiple reports of damaging winds which downed trees and power lines across East Texas, Northwest Louisiana, and Southeast Oklahoma. These storms eventually weakened by early evening as the air mass stabilized in response to the more widespread rain cooled air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on Moran Loop.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Upper-level troughing remained prominent across the Gulf of Mexico with a speed max extending east-northeast from the Bay of Campeche into the northwest Caribbean Sea. A decaying Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) was lifting north through the Atlantic waters while surface troughing extended from the southern Florida Peninsula southwest into the southern Gulf of Mexico. Given the diffluent pattern aloft, subtle vorticity perturbations, the remnant MCV, and the surface trough, plentiful sources for lift were evident across South Florida that allowed for the development of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms. Additionally, plenty of moisture was distributed areawide with rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour. Abundant moisture along with preceding heavy rainfall and antecedent conditions led to widespread flooding across Miami-Dade and Broward counties. Furthermore, increasing low-level shear behind the MCV whipped up a brief tornado in Miami-Dade County and a funnel cloud in Broward County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported flooding on NW 27th Ave and NW 36th St including the SR 112 ramps. A shopping plaza in the area was also experiencing flooding. Roads are impassable by car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough diving southeast across Eastern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas in the northwest flow aloft during the evening through the early morning hours of May 7th-8th, enhanced large scale forcing ahead of an attendant cold front, resulting in a complex of showers and thunderstorms to develop near and ahead of the front. This mesoscale convective system, or MCS, quickly shifted southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the early morning hours of May 8th, strengthening as it encountered greater instability and a strong southerly low level jet. This resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms containing damaging winds, triggering numerous reports of wind damage across these areas. In addition, strong surface winds with gusts up to 50 mph ahead of the complex of showers and thunderstorms also downed several trees given the wet antecedent soil moisture conditions in place from above normal rainfall observed since the start of the year. These storms exited North Louisiana shortly after daybreak on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down onto Highway 154 just south of Gibsland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late-season push of Arctic air brought a freeze and record-breaking cold temperatures across eastern Kentucky May 9-10th, following a strong cold front which pushed through eastern Kentucky late in the evening on May 8th. The Jackson National Weather Service Office, on top of Sugar Camp Mountain, dropped to 30 degrees on the morning of the 9th, setting an all-time record low temperature for the month of May. The previous record was 32 degrees set in 1989 and tied in 1997 and 2004. Jackson also broke the daily record of 35 degrees set in 1983. The other long-standing eastern Kentucky NWS weather recording site at the London-Corbin Airport plummeted to 28 degrees, tying the previous all-time record low temperature for the month of May set in 1963. London also broke the daily record low of 33 set in 1976. Elsewhere across eastern Kentucky, most experienced temperatures in the upper 20s to lower 30s. A few of the higher elevation locations were even colder, including Black Mountain (elevation 4,031 ft.) and Dorton (elevation 2,774 ft.) with lows of 21 and 26 degrees, respectively. ||The intense May sun quickly moderated the anomalously cold airmass during the afternoon of the 9th.  However, the airmass was still cool and dry enough for one more night of sub-freezing temperatures across much of eastern Kentucky into the morning of May 10th. The Jackson National Weather Service Office, located on a thermal belt ridge, dropped to a daily record low of 36 degrees, breaking the previous daily record low of 38 degrees set in 2010. Meanwhile, the London-Corbin Airport dipped to 33 degrees, falling 3 degrees short of the 30 degree daily record set in 1966. Many of the sheltered valleys saw temperatures dipping to between 29 and 32 degrees. Record cool daily maximum temperatures of 54 degrees were also set at the Jackson office on both the 8th and 9th. ||The first night generally featured the coldest sub-freezing temperatures, but the lateness of the frontal passage on the evening of the 8th kept the coldest air from settling over the area for more than a few hours, possibly resulting in a less damaging freeze than what would have typically occurred with cold temperatures of this magnitude. That being said, impacts were still felt, especially in terms of horticulture. Apples were taken out in Rowan County, while Pulaski County had about all of their peaches frozen out. Pears and winter wheat were also damaged across eastern Kentucky.||The last time eastern Kentucky felt temperatures this cold this late in the season was May 10, 1966.

The high then strengthened on May 27 and May 28 resulting in widespread record heat over the region on both days with highs in the San Joaquin Valley mainly between 103 and 107 on both days. Triple digit heat was also observed across portions of the Sierra foothills and Kern County Deserts. Temperatures cooled by several degrees on May 29 and lowered to below seasonal averages by May 30 as the large area high pressure broke down, and a cold front pushed through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime highs ranged between 102 and 106 degrees on May 27 and May 28.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two small but intense bowing thunderstorm clusters moved rapidly east/southeastward across southeast Missouri during the late afternoon hours. Damage surveys confirmed a brief EF-0 tornado, however the most noteworthy events were two macrobursts containing peak winds in the 95 to 110 mph range. Flash flooding of low water crossings  occurred due to repeated thunderstorm activity over the Ozark foothills. Although the bowing clusters of storms resided in relatively stable air to the north of a stationary front over western Tennessee and central Arkansas, occasional damaging wind gusts occurred due to their well-organized nature.

The winds were light enough for a brief period of frost in most places. Low temperatures were in the lower to mid 30's. The main impact of the frost was on horticulture and fruit crops.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Arthur, which was moving over the outer banks of North Carolina, was forecast to continue moving northeastward off the Mid-Atlantic coastline. At the same time, the tail of Arthur, basically a trough of low pressure, extended into the southeastern portion of the country. This also combined with a mid to upper level area of low pressure moving into the Tennessee Valley and a trough of low pressure moving into the eastern Gulf of Mexico which allowed for a south southwesterly flow across South Florida. This allowed for the Gulf coast sea breeze to push inland as the east coast sea breeze remained pushed up against the east coast. This eventually lead to the development of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across all of South Florida. The primary impacts with these storms were heavy rainfall and associated flooding, frequent lightning strikes, small hail, and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several inches of rain, with measured amounts ranging from 3 to 6 inches, and locally higher amounts, caused flooding in portions of Boynton Beach and Ocean Ridge. Law enforcement reported Woolbright Road was closed from Federal Highway to the intracoastal waterway bridge due to heavy rainfall. The Weather Underground station KFLBOYNT1 near Bethesda Hospital East in Boynton Beach measured 5.43 inches of rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rex block characterized by a deep upper-level low across the Tennessee Valley Region and an upper-level high across the Great Lakes Region gave way to an upper-level cold pocket across the southeastern portions of the United states. Simultaneously, a mid-level vorticity lobe rotated across the region which also aided in an increase of convection, especially due to the combination of lingering boundaries and sea breeze formation. Forecast soundings also showed an inverted V as well as favorable DCAPE values, which were supportive for a few damaging wind gusts with the taller, more robust, updrafts contained hail. Furthermore, tornado potential increased with favorable low level winds and shear across land. Finally, with an overall weaker flow aloft and PWATs approaching the 2 inch mark, some localized flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A video via social media reported quarter size hail near Sample Road and the Sawgrass Expressway near Coral Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Upper-level troughing remained prominent across the Gulf of Mexico with a speed max extending east-northeast from the Bay of Campeche into the northwest Caribbean Sea. A decaying Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) was lifting north through the Atlantic waters while surface troughing extended from the southern Florida Peninsula southwest into the southern Gulf of Mexico. Given the diffluent pattern aloft, subtle vorticity perturbations, the remnant MCV, and the surface trough, plentiful sources for lift were evident across South Florida that allowed for the development of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms. Additionally, plenty of moisture was distributed areawide with rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour. Abundant moisture along with preceding heavy rainfall and antecedent conditions led to widespread flooding across Miami-Dade and Broward counties. Furthermore, increasing low-level shear behind the MCV whipped up a brief tornado in Miami-Dade County and a funnel cloud in Broward County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported a funnel cloud in the vicinity of Dania Beach Blvd and US-1 in Dania Beach.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slight severe risk was draped across much of the CWA due to a surface convergent boundary over western counties with an approaching cold front from the north. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving low pressure system drifted across the Ohio Valley on May 18 and 19, bringing several rounds of heavy rain to the eastern reaches of the Commonwealth. The hardest hit areas spanned from the Cumberland Valley to the Bluegrass region where widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6 inches fell over the two day period. This caused several road closures and flooding of low lying areas as points on the Red, Kentucky, and Cumberland Rivers reached minor to moderate flood stage. In Jackson County, a couple of water rescues had to be performed as motorists became trapped.||Flash flooding was confined to the afternoon and evening hours of May 18th across portions of Pulaski and Fleming Counties, while isolated severe thunderstorm winds occurred in Laurel and Jackson Counties. Additionally, a home near Somerset was hit by lightning while mudslides occurred near Bledsoe in Harlan County on U.S. Highway 421, on Kentucky Highway 1110 south of Jackson in Breathitt County, and on Proctor Road near Beattyville in Lee County due to the abundant rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A citizen observed flooding of low lying areas near McKee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough diving southeast across Eastern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas in the northwest flow aloft during the evening through the early morning hours of May 7th-8th, enhanced large scale forcing ahead of an attendant cold front, resulting in a complex of showers and thunderstorms to develop near and ahead of the front. This mesoscale convective system, or MCS, quickly shifted southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the early morning hours of May 8th, strengthening as it encountered greater instability and a strong southerly low level jet. This resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms containing damaging winds, triggering numerous reports of wind damage across these areas. In addition, strong surface winds with gusts up to 50 mph ahead of the complex of showers and thunderstorms also downed several trees given the wet antecedent soil moisture conditions in place from above normal rainfall observed since the start of the year. These storms exited North Louisiana shortly after daybreak on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were blown down on Highway 146 and Highway 148.
