Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge that had been dominant over the Southern Plains and Ark-La-Tex region to start the first couple of days of July had weakened by July 3rd, with a weak upper level disturbance sliding south into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. A complex of showers and thunderstorms that developed over Central and Southern Arkansas during the evening of the 2nd reinforced a weak surface trough southwest into extreme Southeast Oklahoma, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the morning hours of the 3rd, with this boundary focusing an area of compressional heating and moisture pooling throughout the day. As a result, afternoon temperatures climbed into the lower to middle 90s, with limited mixing of dewpoints resulting in oppressive heat indices of 105-110 degrees across extreme Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, extreme Northeast Texas, and Western Louisiana from late morning through the mid afternoon hours. However, showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary by early afternoon, with this complex of storms shifting west southwest across the region during the afternoon, resulting in much cooler conditions and relief to the oppressive heat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South-southwesterly flow allowed for deep tropical moisture to stay in place across South Florida. This prevailing flow also allowed the Gulf sea breeze to progress further inland, pinning the Atlantic sea breeze to the coast, becoming the focus for afternoon showers and thunderstorms. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours.  Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County.  Meanwhile, hailstones as large as 2 inches in diameter caused considerable damage to car dealerships in Savoy and numerous roofs on the east side of Urbana in Champaign County.  The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Carson County started the month of July with severe drought (D2) to extreme drought (D3) conditions in the north to northwest, almost half, of the county. Dryland cotton was not growing in the Texas Panhandle where D2 and D3 conditions were existing. In Carson County, 90 percent of the dryland cotton did not sprout. From about the third week of July some beneficial monsoonal rains dropped 1.79 inches in Panhandle which is about average for the month. This helped erode some of the D2 and D3 conditions going into August with the exception of the far northeast corner of the county. Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels. During the month of July at least one big wildfire was reported due to the dry conditions. No acreage information was available, but 9 different Fire Departments responded to contain the fire and avoid structure damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Saturday, July 11, producing widespread wind damage and very large hail. The first line of storms came through during the morning, producing damaging wind gusts and reports of quarter to ping pong ball size hail from Independence to Tipton Iowa. A wind gust of 65 MPH was measured just west of Independence. The second round of thunderstorms developed as a result of an upper level disturbance interacting with an atmosphere characterized by extremely high instability with modest vertical wind shear. Activity initially formed in north central Iowa, producing golf ball to two inch hail from Fort Dodge to Waterloo Iowa. Eventually, storms made their way towards the Cedar Rapids/Iowa City metro areas, producing widespread wind damage and hail up to baseball size. These storms continued through the Quad Cities metro east towards Princeton, Sterling, and Hennepin Illinois, producing additional reports of wind damage and winds of 70 to 90 mph. Numerous power outages were also reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After almost a two year hiatus, drought conditions returned to the South Plains of West Texas in July. Some areas of the South Plains experienced much below normal rainfall in the spring months. The most extreme deficits occurred in both Yoakum and Terry Counties which saw rainfall amounts between four and five inches below normal. Much of the area in these counties were raised to D2 (Severe Drought) or D3 (Extreme Drought) by the end of July. These same drought levels also covered the extreme southwestern and south-central Texas Panhandle southward into the northern South Plains. These additional areas of drought experienced rainfall deficits around 1.5 inches. The lack of rainfall contributed to the extreme heat that was observed in July. At Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport, an all-time July temperature record was set on the 14th of 111 degrees Fahrenheit. The mean temperature for July was 85.5 degrees Fahrenheit. This value was the second warmest July on record only to the year 2011 when the last D4 (Exceptional Drought) occurred.||Dryland crops had mostly failed by June with the lack of significant rainfall in addition to isolated hail storms destroying crops. Some irrigated crops were generally in poor to very poor condition due to deteriorating soil moisture. Despite the very dry conditions across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle, there was a lack of significant wildfire activity. No known estimates of crop losses were known at this time.

November was another month of mostly below normal rainfall across South Central Texas. Most of the northern half of the area had less than 50% of normal with some places in the northwest having less than 10%. In most of our counties the drought worsened during the month. Bandera, Comal, Gillespie, Kendall, and Kerr Counties entered Extreme (D3) Drought. Bastrop, Bexar, Blanco, Burnet, Caldwell, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Kinney, Lee, Llano, Real, Travis, Val Verde, and Williamson ended the month in Severe (D2) Drought. Uvalde and Zavala remained in D3, and Dimmit, Frio, and Maverick stayed in D2. Medina County with near normal rain actually improved from D3 to D2. Public water systems across the region had instituted some level of water restrictions. The Pecos, Frio, Nueces, Medina, and lower Guadalupe river basins reported much below normal seven-day stream flows at the end of the month. The upper and middle Guadalupe, San Antonio, Blanco, San Marcos. Brazos, and Colorado river basins reported below normal seven-day flows. Reservoirs in the drought areas were below normal with Lake Amistad 44 feet below normal. All of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect except Burnet, Kerr, and Bastrop.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge that had been dominant over the Southern Plains and Ark-La-Tex region to start the first couple of days of July had weakened by July 3rd, with a weak upper level disturbance sliding south into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. A complex of showers and thunderstorms that developed over Central and Southern Arkansas during the evening of the 2nd reinforced a weak surface trough southwest into extreme Southeast Oklahoma, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the morning hours of the 3rd, with this boundary focusing an area of compressional heating and moisture pooling throughout the day. As a result, afternoon temperatures climbed into the lower to middle 90s, with limited mixing of dewpoints resulting in oppressive heat indices of 105-110 degrees across extreme Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, extreme Northeast Texas, and Western Louisiana from late morning through the mid afternoon hours. However, showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary by early afternoon, with this complex of storms shifting west southwest across the region during the afternoon, resulting in much cooler conditions and relief to the oppressive heat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved into the region on the 26th and meandered across the region through the 31st before an unseasonably strong upper level low pressure system moved east of the region. A very moist airmass and slow movement of the upper level system led to periods of very heavy rainfall each day. The most notable heavy rain event occurred across St. Clair County between Osceola and Lowry City. Over 7 inches of rain fell in a period of a few hours during the early morning of the 31st and led to flash flooding which washed out several roads and bridges and shut down the south bound lane of Highway 13. One public observer from Osceola measured over 11 inches of rain from 3 AM to 9 AM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall was reported from several locations across Hickory County. Near Galmey, an amateur radio operator reported 4.40 inches of rain falling between 6 am and noon. The Co-op observer at Pomme De Terre reported 2.20 inches of rainfall and a weather watcher measured a 24 hour rainfall total of 5.52 inches near Cross Timers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Hanna was the first hurricane of the 2020 Atlantic Basin hurricane season and made landfall on the lower Texas coast north of Port Mansfield on the afternoon of the 25th. The tropical wave moved northwest across Cuba into the central Gulf of Mexico where it became a tropical depression on the morning of the 22nd. Tropical Storm Hanna formed late in the evening on the 23rd as it moved west-northwest over the central Gulf of Mexico. Hanna continued to strengthen and became a hurricane on the morning of the 25th around 100 miles east of the Middle Texas coast. Hurricane Hanna turned to the southwest and made landfall over Kenedy County,  between Baffin Bay and Port Mansfield, late in the afternoon on the 25th with a peak intensity of 90 mph and a central pressure of 973 millibars.||Tropical storm force winds occurred along the Middle Texas coast into the eastern portions of the Brush Country from the afternoon of the 25th until the early morning hours of the 26th. Hurricane force gusts occurred over the coastal portion of Kleberg County during the afternoon of the 25th. ||Storm surge from Hanna affected the entire Middle Texas coast from the 25th until the 26th. Storm surge ranged from 1 to 3 feet above ground level for the coastal areas of Aransas, Calhoun, and Refugio Counties. Storm surge ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 feet above ground level for coastal areas of San Patricio, Nueces, and Kleberg Counties. ||The highest surge was at Bob Hall Pier with a reading of 5.48 feet mean higher high water. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours.  Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County.  Meanwhile, hailstones as large as 2 inches in diameter caused considerable damage to car dealerships in Savoy and numerous roofs on the east side of Urbana in Champaign County.  The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous large trees and tree branches were blown down.  A power pole was broken, and the roof of a shed was damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At least some portion of the western Oklahoma Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since November of 2019. After the drought worsened and peaked in June, significant improvement occurred across the central and eastern portions of the Oklahoma Panhandle in July where monsoon rainfall led to 150 to 300 percent above normal rainfall. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 4 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement in those areas. However, some of the western Oklahoma Panhandle experienced only 50 to 75 percent of normal rainfall in July which lead to additional deficits of 1-2 inches for the month. Given this, Extreme Drought (D3) persisted in parts of the far western Oklahoma Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most of the county was experiencing extreme drought (D3) early in July. Beneficial rainfall improved drought conditions in the south, although abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought remained (D1).  Extreme drought (D3) persisted through July across the far north where less rainfall occurred.

There was even a very small area, probably only about 1% of the county that was in exceptional drought (D4) in the far northwest initially. Beneficial monsoon rainfall developed and increase around the third week of July and continued through the end of the month. Rainfall in Goodwell was well above normal by the end of the month with 6.77 inches of precipitation measured. Guymon's monthly precipitation came in at 5.17 inches. Most of the county had reduced its drought severity by 2 categories. By the end of the month, most of the county had improved to abnormally dry (D0) status with the area between Texhoma, Goodwell, and Guymon were completely removed from all drought categories.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) conditions dominated the south to southeast portions of the county through the first half of the month with most of the rest of the county in severe drought (D2). The most beneficial rainfall from monsoonal moisture fell during the 3rd week of the month. 1.20 inches of the 1.82 inches that fell in for Borger, occurred on the 16th, 19th, and 20th of the month. A small portion or D3 to D2 still existed in the far southeast corner of the county going into August.  In July, a couple of wildfires were started by lightning due to the dryness of vegetation. About 9000 to 10,000 acres burned from two different fires started by lightning.

Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening as an upper level disturbance in northwest flow aloft. The strongly sheared environment led to rotating storms, which supported the production of very large hail and damaging winds across western, northern and central parts of the Panhandle. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Eta passed northwest through the middle Florida Keys on November 8 through 9, 2020.  Primary impacts from wind occurred as result of a primary rain band which drifted very slowly north through the Upper Florida Keys.  Peak wind gusts were mostly in the 50 to 60 mph range, downing trees and large tree limbs, utility lines, and a billboard. One residence was destroyed by a fallen tree resulting in 1 minor injury. Two other residential structures were significantly damaged, with three inaccessible  due to blocked streets. About 20 separate power outages affected about 1,000 customers, mostly in Key Largo. Storm Surge flooding was generally in the 1.5 to 2.5 foot range, producing significant street flooding in oceanside Key Largo neighborhoods.  The northbound right-of-way was damaged including major erosion, loss of riprap, and about 3,000 feet of fencing along northbound U.S. Highway 1 along the west end of Barnes Sound and Manatee Bay.  Minor overwash occurred in the middle Florida Keys at Key Colony Beach, along with yard and dock flooding along the Florida Bay side of Marathon. Widespread rainfall of 3.5 to over 8 inches was measured throughout the Keys, with the highest totals in Key Largo.  Damages were estimated near $500K due to mostly from homes damaged by falling trees and tree limbs, as well as utility damage. Storm Surge damage near $100K due to wave action on top of a minor storm surge to the U.S Highway 1 right-of-way.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds of 25 to 40 mph with frequent gusts of 40 to 60 mph were observed throughout the upper Florida Keys, with the strongest winds measured at a sustained speed of 41 mph at a private residential development in Rock Harbor with a peak gust of 58 mph. Wind gusts in excess of 50 mph were also measured at the Florida Keys Electric Cooperative Substation at Jewfish Creek, as well as at a residence on Plantation Key. Numerous trees and power lines were downed, with one house destroyed by a fallen tree in Key Largo along with one injury.  Approximately 1,000 customers were without power, mostly in Key Largo.  One wooden-post billboard was downed, with County Road 905, also known as Card Sound Road, blocked in several places due to downed trees between mile markers 3 and 8.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After almost a two year hiatus, drought conditions returned to the South Plains of West Texas in July. Some areas of the South Plains experienced much below normal rainfall in the spring months. The most extreme deficits occurred in both Yoakum and Terry Counties which saw rainfall amounts between four and five inches below normal. Much of the area in these counties were raised to D2 (Severe Drought) or D3 (Extreme Drought) by the end of July. These same drought levels also covered the extreme southwestern and south-central Texas Panhandle southward into the northern South Plains. These additional areas of drought experienced rainfall deficits around 1.5 inches. The lack of rainfall contributed to the extreme heat that was observed in July. At Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport, an all-time July temperature record was set on the 14th of 111 degrees Fahrenheit. The mean temperature for July was 85.5 degrees Fahrenheit. This value was the second warmest July on record only to the year 2011 when the last D4 (Exceptional Drought) occurred.||Dryland crops had mostly failed by June with the lack of significant rainfall in addition to isolated hail storms destroying crops. Some irrigated crops were generally in poor to very poor condition due to deteriorating soil moisture. Despite the very dry conditions across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle, there was a lack of significant wildfire activity. No known estimates of crop losses were known at this time.

After almost a two year hiatus, drought conditions returned to the South Plains of West Texas in July. Some areas of the South Plains experienced much below normal rainfall in the spring months. The most extreme deficits occurred in both Yoakum and Terry Counties which saw rainfall amounts between four and five inches below normal. Much of the area in these counties were raised to D2 (Severe Drought) or D3 (Extreme Drought) by the end of July. These same drought levels also covered the extreme southwestern and south-central Texas Panhandle southward into the northern South Plains. These additional areas of drought experienced rainfall deficits around 1.5 inches. The lack of rainfall contributed to the extreme heat that was observed in July. At Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport, an all-time July temperature record was set on the 14th of 111 degrees Fahrenheit. The mean temperature for July was 85.5 degrees Fahrenheit. This value was the second warmest July on record only to the year 2011 when the last D4 (Exceptional Drought) occurred.||Dryland crops had mostly failed by June with the lack of significant rainfall in addition to isolated hail storms destroying crops. Some irrigated crops were generally in poor to very poor condition due to deteriorating soil moisture. Despite the very dry conditions across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle, there was a lack of significant wildfire activity. No known estimates of crop losses were known at this time.

November was another month of mostly below normal rainfall across South Central Texas. Most of the northern half of the area had less than 50% of normal with some places in the northwest having less than 10%. In most of our counties the drought worsened during the month. Bandera, Comal, Gillespie, Kendall, and Kerr Counties entered Extreme (D3) Drought. Bastrop, Bexar, Blanco, Burnet, Caldwell, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Kinney, Lee, Llano, Real, Travis, Val Verde, and Williamson ended the month in Severe (D2) Drought. Uvalde and Zavala remained in D3, and Dimmit, Frio, and Maverick stayed in D2. Medina County with near normal rain actually improved from D3 to D2. Public water systems across the region had instituted some level of water restrictions. The Pecos, Frio, Nueces, Medina, and lower Guadalupe river basins reported much below normal seven-day stream flows at the end of the month. The upper and middle Guadalupe, San Antonio, Blanco, San Marcos. Brazos, and Colorado river basins reported below normal seven-day flows. Reservoirs in the drought areas were below normal with Lake Amistad 44 feet below normal. All of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect except Burnet, Kerr, and Bastrop.

An upper level ridge that had been dominant over the Southern Plains and Ark-La-Tex region to start the first couple of days of July had weakened by July 3rd, with a weak upper level disturbance sliding south into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. A complex of showers and thunderstorms that developed over Central and Southern Arkansas during the evening of the 2nd reinforced a weak surface trough southwest into extreme Southeast Oklahoma, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the morning hours of the 3rd, with this boundary focusing an area of compressional heating and moisture pooling throughout the day. As a result, afternoon temperatures climbed into the lower to middle 90s, with limited mixing of dewpoints resulting in oppressive heat indices of 105-110 degrees across extreme Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, extreme Northeast Texas, and Western Louisiana from late morning through the mid afternoon hours. However, showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary by early afternoon, with this complex of storms shifting west southwest across the region during the afternoon, resulting in much cooler conditions and relief to the oppressive heat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved into the region on the 26th and meandered across the region through the 31st before an unseasonably strong upper level low pressure system moved east of the region. A very moist airmass and slow movement of the upper level system led to periods of very heavy rainfall each day. The most notable heavy rain event occurred across St. Clair County between Osceola and Lowry City. Over 7 inches of rain fell in a period of a few hours during the early morning of the 31st and led to flash flooding which washed out several roads and bridges and shut down the south bound lane of Highway 13. One public observer from Osceola measured over 11 inches of rain from 3 AM to 9 AM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous locations across Morgan County received more than 2 inches of rain over a 24 hour period. The heaviest rains fell in the Stover and Versailles areas with between 2.00 and 4.51 inches of rainfall measured by Co-op observers, Mesonet stations and the public.

Extensive line of thunderstorms brought widespread severe wind to much of south central Nebraska and portions of north central Kansas on this date. This event will likely go down as the most widespread severe weather event of the spring and summer of 2020 for the Hastings County Warning Area (CWA). Thunderstorms developed along a cold front across north central Nebraska, and also within a zone of low level upslope flow over western Nebraska and northeast Colorado, during the early evening hours of July 8th. Both areas of development initially contained line segments and embedded supercells, posing risks for all severe hazards, but quickly organized into two separate lines of convection, or quasi linear convective systems (QLCSs). By 9pm CDT, one line extended roughly west to east from Thedford, NE to O'Neill, NE and was moving southeast, while the other line extended roughly north to south from near Thedford, NE to just west of McCook, NE and was moving mainly east. Shortly thereafter, both lines began to merge together into one coherent line and produced several instances of 60-75 mph wind gusts and isolated severe hail north/northwest of the CWA. Thunderstorms increased in organization into a bow echo over Furnas and Gosper Counties in Nebraska, then entered far western/northwestern portions of north central Kansas between 10:30-11pm CDT. By 11pm CDT, the QLCS had taken on an ���S��� shape, slanting southwest to northeast. The greatest concentration of severe wind reports occurred north of the state line, however, several severe wind reports were also reported roughly along and north of Highway 36 between 11pm CDT on July 8th and 1am CDT on July 9th as forward speed increased dramatically. Peak wind gusts across north central Kansas generally remained 60-65mph. The only known damage was to a roof of a mobile home in Mitchell County, though at least minor tree and crop damage likely occurred across at least portions of the area as well. The leading edge of the QLCS, and associated peak wind threat, shifted east and southeast of the CWA by 1AM CDT, though lingering stratiform rain as well as a northwest to southeast band of thunderstorms near the state line continued for a few more hours. Severe hail associated with this activity remained just north of the state line, over Furnas County, where regenerating thunderstorms were most intense.||Meteorologically speaking, this severe wind event was driven largely by a cold front interacting with a strongly unstable airmass due to steep mid level lapse rates, strong heating, and moist boundary layer. Initially cellular activity quickly grew upscale into line segments owing to the linear forcing along the cold front and generally outflow dominated activity, with peak DCAPE values in excess of 1500 J/kg. The primary shortwave trough responsible for the cold front remained well north of the area, near the Montana/Canadian border, but several weak perturbations moving west to east over the cold front likely aided in thunderstorm development as well. A distinct mesoscale convective vortex, modest deep layer shear of 30-35 knots, and an intensifying southerly low level jet up to 45 knots sustained the severe convection well past sunset. Finally, it's worth noting that an impressive surface pressure rise/fall couplet of at least 3mb/2hr accompanied the QLCS across the CWA between 05Z and 07Z.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Hanna was the first hurricane of the 2020 Atlantic Basin hurricane season and made landfall on the lower Texas coast north of Port Mansfield on the afternoon of the 25th. Hanna was the first hurricane to make landfall in Texas since Hurricane Harvey. ||Hanna began as a tropical wave, first noted for possible development when it was near Hispaniola on the 19th. The tropical wave moved northwest across Cuba into the central Gulf of Mexico where it became a tropical depression on the morning of the 22nd. Tropical Storm Hanna formed late in the evening on the 23rd as it moved west-northwest over the central Gulf of Mexico. Hanna continued to strengthen and became a hurricane on the morning of the 25th around 100 miles east of the Middle Texas coast. Hurricane Hanna turned to the southwest and made landfall over Kenedy County,  between Baffin Bay and Port Mansfield, late in the afternoon on the 25th with a peak intensity of 90 mph and a central pressure of 973 millibars.||Tropical storm force winds occurred along the Middle Texas coast into the eastern portions of the Brush Country from the afternoon of the 25th until the early morning hours of the 26th. Hurricane force gusts occurred over the coastal portion of Kleberg County during the afternoon of the 25th. ||Storm surge from Hanna affected the entire Middle Texas coast from the 25th until the 26th. Storm surge ranged from 1 to 3 feet above ground level for the coastal areas of Aransas, Calhoun, and Refugio Counties. Storm surge ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 feet above ground level for coastal areas of San Patricio, Nueces, and Kleberg Counties. ||The highest surge was at Bob Hall Pier with a reading of 5.48 feet mean higher high water. Storm surge damaged numerous piers and docks in Nueces and Corpus Christi Bays south to Baffin Bay. Storm surge damaged navigation markers in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. Some parts of the Corpus Christi marina were damaged. Bob Hall Pier sustained significant damage with the t-head parts of the pier being destroyed. Damage from Hurricane Hanna was estimated to be around 54 million dollars.||Minor wind damage occurred across the Coastal Bend as tropical storm force winds caused power outages and minor tree damage. There were three tornadoes over the Coastal Bend associated with the outer bands of Hurricane Hanna. The three tornadoes were weak (EF0). The tornadoes affected the communities of Bonnie View, Pernitas Point, and Lagarto.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tide levels reached 3 to 4.5 feet above ground level with the storm surge. Surge damaged Bob Hall Pier with the t-head parts being destroyed. Storm surge destroyed the parking lot at Bob Hall Pier.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South-southwesterly flow allowed for deep tropical moisture to stay in place across South Florida. This prevailing flow also allowed the Gulf sea breeze to progress further inland, pinning the Atlantic sea breeze to the coast, becoming the focus for afternoon showers and thunderstorms. Broad high pressure remained in control, though a weak low pressure lingered around the MS/AL coastline with an associated surface boundary stretching from east TX through the FL panhandle and into the western Atlantic. This allowed for an increase in thunderstorms along the east coast that brought gusty winds and hail to portions of Broward County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported a large outdoor contraption, consisting of mesh netting well-attached to a solid wooden enclosure, was fully lofted and tilted vertically, colliding with backyard facing side of a house. Mesh was damaged. Backyard lawn recreational items also toppled. This thunderstorm wind damage was in association with a microburst. Estimated wind gusts near 60 mph based primarily on magnitude of damage as well as strength of storm observed on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall containing severe wind gusts passed through portions of the Lower Florida Keys, with maximum wind gusts occurring on Cudjoe Key.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust of 50 knots, or 58 mph, was measured on Cudjoe Key near the southern end of Sawyer Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Lightning West wildfire began about twelve miles east southeast of Plemons Texas in Hutchinson County around 1650CST. The wildfire consumed six thousand five hundred and ten acres. The cause of the wildfire was determined to be from lightning. There were two homes and two other structures threatened by the wildfire but were saved. There were also no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The Texas A&M Forest Service along with the Booker VFD, the Fritch VFD, Hardin County ESD #5, the Skellytown VFD, Borger Fire Department, Crutch Ranch VFD, the Hoover VFD, Miami/Roberts County VFD, Panhandle Fire Department, Perryton Fire Department, and White Deer VFD responded to the wildfire. The wildfire was contained around 2000CST on July 12 and brought under control around 1500CST on July 16.

The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought (D2) to extreme drought (D3) existed in the southwest half of the county going into the first week of July. Some beneficial monsoonal rainfall fell in the northern half of the county eroding the the D2 conditions in the portions of the northwest while D2 and D3 conditions began to appear in all of the southern areas along the county line into Gray County.  Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Kentucky sat under the front of an upper ridge as a surface low advanced toward the state. This low anchored a warm front to the east and cold front to the west and caused thunderstorms to breakout across central Kentucky as the system moved through the area. The storms produced wind and hail damage across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A residence on Huntsville-Quality Road was struck by lightning and caught on fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary frontal boundary triggered several rounds of showers and thunderstorms on July 21st.  One cluster of storms tracked through east-central Illinois during the late morning, blowing down a few trees and power lines across portions of Piatt and Champaign counties.  Additional convection developed further west toward midday, with a line of storms then progressing eastward across much of central Illinois during the afternoon.  Scattered wind damage occurred with this line, while one cell produced an EF-1 tornado near Auburn in Sangamon County.

Diurnally driven showers and thunderstorms formed during the afternoon hours and caused wind damage across parts of the Metroplex. Lightning struck a teenager in Dallas County, and the male passed away a week later.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed power poles were reported near Saginaw Boulevard and Boaz.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed tree limbs and shingles off of roofs was reported via mPing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During a time without any major weather systems moving through the region, a moist atmosphere with differential heating and remaining outflows from earlier thunderstorms was enough for thunderstorms and heavy rain to develop across central Kentucky. This resulted in widespread wind damage, flooding, and even fires from lightning. An elderly man drowned and his wife was injured trying to drive through flood waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was water in one home, and a private bridge to get to other houses was under water on Rush Branch Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed along a boundary from southeast South Dakota into northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota, producing damaging wind and spotty large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust to 60 mph measured by hand-held anemometer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mixture of rain and snow showers developed behind a strong cold front and upper level trough during the early afternoon hours. The rain become all snow as temperatures fell into the upper 20s (atop the Cumberland Plateau) to lower 30s in valley areas. Snow accumulations of 1/2 to 1 inch were reported, mainly on grassy and elevated surfaces. The snow ended during the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulation of 0.5 inch was reported at 6.1 NNW of Fayetteville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong cold front moved south through the region. A line of strong to severe storms developed ahead of the cold front. Some of the storms produced widespread wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs and power lines around town.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down a large tree onto I-64 east bound lane. In DuBois, several small trees were blown down around town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several low level boundaries were across the local forecast area including a wake trough axis post-Isaias across south Georgia and an outflow boundary stalled near the I-95 corridor of NE FL. With daytime heating, high moisture content (PWAT 2 inches) and steeper mid level lapse rates (MU 7.4 degC), scattered strong to severe storms developed along and near the boundaries. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Eta passed northwest through the middle Florida Keys on November 8 through 9, 2020.  Primary impacts from wind occurred as result of a primary rain band which drifted very slowly north through the Upper Florida Keys.  Peak wind gusts were mostly in the 50 to 60 mph range, downing trees and large tree limbs, utility lines, and a billboard. One residence was destroyed by a fallen tree resulting in 1 minor injury. Two other residential structures were significantly damaged, with three inaccessible  due to blocked streets. About 20 separate power outages affected about 1,000 customers, mostly in Key Largo. Storm Surge flooding was generally in the 1.5 to 2.5 foot range, producing significant street flooding in oceanside Key Largo neighborhoods.  The northbound right-of-way was damaged including major erosion, loss of riprap, and about 3,000 feet of fencing along northbound U.S. Highway 1 along the west end of Barnes Sound and Manatee Bay.  Minor overwash occurred in the middle Florida Keys at Key Colony Beach, along with yard and dock flooding along the Florida Bay side of Marathon. Widespread rainfall of 3.5 to over 8 inches was measured throughout the Keys, with the highest totals in Key Largo.  Damages were estimated near $500K due to mostly from homes damaged by falling trees and tree limbs, as well as utility damage. Storm Surge damage near $100K due to wave action on top of a minor storm surge to the U.S Highway 1 right-of-way.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm force wind gusts were mainly due to isolated rain squalls occurring well in advance to the northwest of the center of circulation. Peak winds were measured sustained at 49 mph with a gust to 56 mph at the USCG Sector Key West.  Isolated power outages to about 100 customers were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Saturday, July 11, producing widespread wind damage and very large hail. The first line of storms came through during the morning, producing damaging wind gusts and reports of quarter to ping pong ball size hail from Independence to Tipton Iowa. A wind gust of 65 MPH was measured just west of Independence. The second round of thunderstorms developed as a result of an upper level disturbance interacting with an atmosphere characterized by extremely high instability with modest vertical wind shear. Activity initially formed in north central Iowa, producing golf ball to two inch hail from Fort Dodge to Waterloo Iowa. Eventually, storms made their way towards the Cedar Rapids/Iowa City metro areas, producing widespread wind damage and hail up to baseball size. These storms continued through the Quad Cities metro east towards Princeton, Sterling, and Hennepin Illinois, producing additional reports of wind damage and winds of 70 to 90 mph. Numerous power outages were also reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated 60 mph winds also reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After almost a two year hiatus, drought conditions returned to the South Plains of West Texas in July. Some areas of the South Plains experienced much below normal rainfall in the spring months. The most extreme deficits occurred in both Yoakum and Terry Counties which saw rainfall amounts between four and five inches below normal. Much of the area in these counties were raised to D2 (Severe Drought) or D3 (Extreme Drought) by the end of July. These same drought levels also covered the extreme southwestern and south-central Texas Panhandle southward into the northern South Plains. These additional areas of drought experienced rainfall deficits around 1.5 inches. The lack of rainfall contributed to the extreme heat that was observed in July. At Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport, an all-time July temperature record was set on the 14th of 111 degrees Fahrenheit. The mean temperature for July was 85.5 degrees Fahrenheit. This value was the second warmest July on record only to the year 2011 when the last D4 (Exceptional Drought) occurred.||Dryland crops had mostly failed by June with the lack of significant rainfall in addition to isolated hail storms destroying crops. Some irrigated crops were generally in poor to very poor condition due to deteriorating soil moisture. Despite the very dry conditions across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle, there was a lack of significant wildfire activity. No known estimates of crop losses were known at this time.

November was another month of mostly below normal rainfall across South Central Texas. Most of the northern half of the area had less than 50% of normal with some places in the northwest having less than 10%. In most of our counties the drought worsened during the month. Bandera, Comal, Gillespie, Kendall, and Kerr Counties entered Extreme (D3) Drought. Bastrop, Bexar, Blanco, Burnet, Caldwell, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Kinney, Lee, Llano, Real, Travis, Val Verde, and Williamson ended the month in Severe (D2) Drought. Uvalde and Zavala remained in D3, and Dimmit, Frio, and Maverick stayed in D2. Medina County with near normal rain actually improved from D3 to D2. Public water systems across the region had instituted some level of water restrictions. The Pecos, Frio, Nueces, Medina, and lower Guadalupe river basins reported much below normal seven-day stream flows at the end of the month. The upper and middle Guadalupe, San Antonio, Blanco, San Marcos. Brazos, and Colorado river basins reported below normal seven-day flows. Reservoirs in the drought areas were below normal with Lake Amistad 44 feet below normal. All of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect except Burnet, Kerr, and Bastrop.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge that had been dominant over the Southern Plains and Ark-La-Tex region to start the first couple of days of July had weakened by July 3rd, with a weak upper level disturbance sliding south into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. A complex of showers and thunderstorms that developed over Central and Southern Arkansas during the evening of the 2nd reinforced a weak surface trough southwest into extreme Southeast Oklahoma, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the morning hours of the 3rd, with this boundary focusing an area of compressional heating and moisture pooling throughout the day. As a result, afternoon temperatures climbed into the lower to middle 90s, with limited mixing of dewpoints resulting in oppressive heat indices of 105-110 degrees across extreme Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, extreme Northeast Texas, and Western Louisiana from late morning through the mid afternoon hours. However, showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary by early afternoon, with this complex of storms shifting west southwest across the region during the afternoon, resulting in much cooler conditions and relief to the oppressive heat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South-southwesterly flow allowed for deep tropical moisture to stay in place across South Florida. This prevailing flow also allowed the Gulf sea breeze to progress further inland, pinning the Atlantic sea breeze to the coast, becoming the focus for afternoon showers and thunderstorms. The presence of a mid-level trough and attendant short wave pushing through South Florida allowed for an increase in thunderstorms along the east coast that brought gusty winds, heavy rainfall, flooding, and hail to portions of Broward, Palm Beach, and Miami-Dade counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter called the NWS Miami to report quarter size hail at the intersection of Belvedere Road and Interstate 95. This was associated with a weak-supercell storm that crossed the West Palm Beach area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Campbell Road wildfire began around 1801CST about twelve miles north northeast of Skellytown Texas in Hutchinson County. There was a report that one home was threatened by the wildfire but was saved, otherwise there were no reports of any homes or other structures threatened. There was a report of one injury, however no fatalities were reported. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At least some portion of the western Oklahoma Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since November of 2019. After the drought worsened and peaked in June, significant improvement occurred across the central and eastern portions of the Oklahoma Panhandle in July where monsoon rainfall led to 150 to 300 percent above normal rainfall. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 4 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement in those areas. However, some of the western Oklahoma Panhandle experienced only 50 to 75 percent of normal rainfall in July which lead to additional deficits of 1-2 inches for the month of July. Given this, Extreme Drought (D3) persisted in parts of the far western Oklahoma Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The western half of Beaver County was severe drought (D2) with small areas in the northwest and southwest in extreme drought (D3) going into July. The eastern half was only in moderate drought (D1) going into the month of July. For the first part of July most of the county degraded into severe drought (D2), although the D3 in the northwest did improve with some beneficial rainfall in the beginning of the month. During the third week of July, the county started to get enough rainfall to eliminate D2 conditions across the entire county. Abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought (D1) conditions remained with the worse conditions noted across the northwest quarter of the county as Beaver and Slapout ended the month with just under 2 inches of rainfall which is just below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hemphill County were not so lucky in receiving monsoonal rainfall during the month of July as some nearby counties did. Just enough rain fell to roughly maintain severe drought (D2) in the southern portion of the county while only seeing a slight improvement in the north to the moderate drought (D1) conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracked from near Kansas City on the morning of July 15th to southern Lake Michigan by midnight on July 16th.  The low interacted with an unstable and very moist environment to produce a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) over eastern Kansas into Missouri, which then pushed into west-central Illinois by the mid to late morning of July 15th.  Several rounds of convection moved across the Illinois River Valley through the afternoon, producing heavy rain and isolated wind damage.  The heaviest rainfall of 5 to 7 inches was focused across Tazewell, Woodford, and far eastern Peoria counties where significant flash flooding occurred.  In addition, 5 weak tornadoes touched down...including 2 in Tazewell County, 1 in McLean County, 1 in Morgan County, and 1 in Montgomery County which then crossed into southern Sangamon County.  Minor damage was reported with some of the tornadoes: however, no injuries or deaths occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two inches of rain fell in about an hour, resulting in numerous flooded streets across Pekin.  Due to additional rainfall, water continued to rise through the afternoon and early evening with up to one foot of water reported on many roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Eta passed northwest through the middle Florida Keys on November 8 through 9, 2020.  Primary impacts from wind occurred as result of a primary rain band which drifted very slowly north through the Upper Florida Keys.  Peak wind gusts were mostly in the 50 to 60 mph range, downing trees and large tree limbs, utility lines, and a billboard. One residence was destroyed by a fallen tree resulting in 1 minor injury. Two other residential structures were significantly damaged, with three inaccessible  due to blocked streets. About 20 separate power outages affected about 1,000 customers, mostly in Key Largo. Storm Surge flooding was generally in the 1.5 to 2.5 foot range, producing significant street flooding in oceanside Key Largo neighborhoods.  The northbound right-of-way was damaged including major erosion, loss of riprap, and about 3,000 feet of fencing along northbound U.S. Highway 1 along the west end of Barnes Sound and Manatee Bay.  Minor overwash occurred in the middle Florida Keys at Key Colony Beach, along with yard and dock flooding along the Florida Bay side of Marathon. Widespread rainfall of 3.5 to over 8 inches was measured throughout the Keys, with the highest totals in Key Largo.  Damages were estimated near $500K due to mostly from homes damaged by falling trees and tree limbs, as well as utility damage. Storm Surge damage near $100K due to wave action on top of a minor storm surge to the U.S Highway 1 right-of-way.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm Surge flooding of 1.5 to 2.0 feet above MHHW was noted oceanside of Key Largo, as well as the western side of Barnes Sound and Manatee Bay.  Oceanside neighborhoods were inundated by up to one foot, along with flooding impassible to vehicles in the parking lots of a resort along the north side of Jewfish Creek.  Minor overwash and a debris line was noted along Sea Oats Beach, an exposed oceanfront portion of U.S. Highway 1 in Lower Matecumbe Key.  Wave action estimated around 4 feet produced severe erosion on along the northbound right-of-way of U.S. Highway 1 south of Manatee Bay, destroying 3,000 feet of chain link fence as well as producing potholes and loss of protective riprap.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Organized clusters of strong to isolated severe thunderstorms moved into southwest Illinois during the late afternoon and evening. A 500 mb disturbance over northwest Missouri moved east-southeast toward west central Illinois during the afternoon. An outflow boundary from morning storms was the focus for thunderstorm development in east central Missouri. These storms propagated southeast across southern Illinois in the evening, fed by a very warm and moist air mass. Partial sunshine resulted in a corridor of strong instability, with mixed layer cape approaching 3500 j/kg. Moderately strong winds aloft associated with the upper level disturbance contributed to the evolution of an organized storm cluster that crossed southwest Illinois in the evening. The storms slowed down later in the evening, resulting in persistent heavy rain and local flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Saturday, July 11, producing widespread wind damage and very large hail. The first line of storms came through during the morning, producing damaging wind gusts and reports of quarter to ping pong ball size hail from Independence to Tipton Iowa. A wind gust of 65 MPH was measured just west of Independence. The second round of thunderstorms developed as a result of an upper level disturbance interacting with an atmosphere characterized by extremely high instability with modest vertical wind shear. Activity initially formed in north central Iowa, producing golf ball to two inch hail from Fort Dodge to Waterloo Iowa. Eventually, storms made their way towards the Cedar Rapids/Iowa City metro areas, producing widespread wind damage and hail up to baseball size. These storms continued through the Quad Cities metro east towards Princeton, Sterling, and Hennepin Illinois, producing additional reports of wind damage and winds of 70 to 90 mph. Numerous power outages were also reported.

After almost a two year hiatus, drought conditions returned to the South Plains of West Texas in July. Some areas of the South Plains experienced much below normal rainfall in the spring months. The most extreme deficits occurred in both Yoakum and Terry Counties which saw rainfall amounts between four and five inches below normal. Much of the area in these counties were raised to D2 (Severe Drought) or D3 (Extreme Drought) by the end of July. These same drought levels also covered the extreme southwestern and south-central Texas Panhandle southward into the northern South Plains. These additional areas of drought experienced rainfall deficits around 1.5 inches. The lack of rainfall contributed to the extreme heat that was observed in July. At Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport, an all-time July temperature record was set on the 14th of 111 degrees Fahrenheit. The mean temperature for July was 85.5 degrees Fahrenheit. This value was the second warmest July on record only to the year 2011 when the last D4 (Exceptional Drought) occurred.||Dryland crops had mostly failed by June with the lack of significant rainfall in addition to isolated hail storms destroying crops. Some irrigated crops were generally in poor to very poor condition due to deteriorating soil moisture. Despite the very dry conditions across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle, there was a lack of significant wildfire activity. No known estimates of crop losses were known at this time.

November was another month of mostly below normal rainfall across South Central Texas. Most of the northern half of the area had less than 50% of normal with some places in the northwest having less than 10%. In most of our counties the drought worsened during the month. Bandera, Comal, Gillespie, Kendall, and Kerr Counties entered Extreme (D3) Drought. Bastrop, Bexar, Blanco, Burnet, Caldwell, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Kinney, Lee, Llano, Real, Travis, Val Verde, and Williamson ended the month in Severe (D2) Drought. Uvalde and Zavala remained in D3, and Dimmit, Frio, and Maverick stayed in D2. Medina County with near normal rain actually improved from D3 to D2. Public water systems across the region had instituted some level of water restrictions. The Pecos, Frio, Nueces, Medina, and lower Guadalupe river basins reported much below normal seven-day stream flows at the end of the month. The upper and middle Guadalupe, San Antonio, Blanco, San Marcos. Brazos, and Colorado river basins reported below normal seven-day flows. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge that had been dominant over the Southern Plains and Ark-La-Tex region to start the first couple of days of July had weakened by July 3rd, with a weak upper level disturbance sliding south into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. A complex of showers and thunderstorms that developed over Central and Southern Arkansas during the evening of the 2nd reinforced a weak surface trough southwest into extreme Southeast Oklahoma, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the morning hours of the 3rd, with this boundary focusing an area of compressional heating and moisture pooling throughout the day. As a result, afternoon temperatures climbed into the lower to middle 90s, with limited mixing of dewpoints resulting in oppressive heat indices of 105-110 degrees across extreme Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, extreme Northeast Texas, and Western Louisiana from late morning through the mid afternoon hours. However, showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary by early afternoon, with this complex of storms shifting west southwest across the region during the afternoon, resulting in much cooler conditions and relief to the oppressive heat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gray County started out the month with severe drought (D2) in the northern half to two thirds of the county. July was very dry for Gray County and extreme drought spread across the northern portions of the county. A small portion of the southern part of the county managed to stay with abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought (D1) as just enough rainfall fell to keep conditions worsening.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracked from near Kansas City on the morning of July 15th to southern Lake Michigan by midnight on July 16th.  The low interacted with an unstable and very moist environment to produce a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) over eastern Kansas into Missouri, which then pushed into west-central Illinois by the mid to late morning of July 15th.  Several rounds of convection moved across the Illinois River Valley through the afternoon, producing heavy rain and isolated wind damage.  The heaviest rainfall of 5 to 7 inches was focused across Tazewell, Woodford, and far eastern Peoria counties where significant flash flooding occurred.  In addition, 5 weak tornadoes touched down...including 2 in Tazewell County, 1 in McLean County, 1 in Morgan County, and 1 in Montgomery County which then crossed into southern Sangamon County.  Minor damage was reported with some of the tornadoes: however, no injuries or deaths occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous roads were flooded with up to one foot of water in Morton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Eta passed northwest through the middle Florida Keys on November 8 through 9, 2020.  Primary impacts from wind occurred as result of a primary rain band which drifted very slowly north through the Upper Florida Keys.  Peak wind gusts were mostly in the 50 to 60 mph range, downing trees and large tree limbs, utility lines, and a billboard. One residence was destroyed by a fallen tree resulting in 1 minor injury. Two other residential structures were significantly damaged, with three inaccessible  due to blocked streets. About 20 separate power outages affected about 1,000 customers, mostly in Key Largo. Storm Surge flooding was generally in the 1.5 to 2.5 foot range, producing significant street flooding in oceanside Key Largo neighborhoods.  The northbound right-of-way was damaged including major erosion, loss of riprap, and about 3,000 feet of fencing along northbound U.S. Highway 1 along the west end of Barnes Sound and Manatee Bay.  Minor overwash occurred in the middle Florida Keys at Key Colony Beach, along with yard and dock flooding along the Florida Bay side of Marathon. Widespread rainfall of 3.5 to over 8 inches was measured throughout the Keys, with the highest totals in Key Largo.  Damages were estimated near $500K due to mostly from homes damaged by falling trees and tree limbs, as well as utility damage. Storm Surge damage near $100K due to wave action on top of a minor storm surge to the U.S Highway 1 right-of-way.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A rise in water levels occurred within a few hours of the maximum northeast winds along the Bayside of Marathon, with water levels peaking about 2.3 feet above MHHW at Stirrup Key.  Water covered docks and inundated waterfront yards, however no significant flooding was observed in area streets.  Minor erosion occurred several hours prior at Key Colony Beach.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Organized clusters of strong to isolated severe thunderstorms moved into southwest Illinois during the late afternoon and evening. A 500 mb disturbance over northwest Missouri moved east-southeast toward west central Illinois during the afternoon. An outflow boundary from morning storms was the focus for thunderstorm development in east central Missouri. These storms propagated southeast across southern Illinois in the evening, fed by a very warm and moist air mass. Partial sunshine resulted in a corridor of strong instability, with mixed layer cape approaching 3500 j/kg. Moderately strong winds aloft associated with the upper level disturbance contributed to the evolution of an organized storm cluster that crossed southwest Illinois in the evening. The storms slowed down later in the evening, resulting in persistent heavy rain and local flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was over a street in Cutler. Water was coming out of ditches and into yards. At least one underpass and a few roads were flooded in Pinckneyville. Barricades were put up. Beaucoup Creek was out of its banks.

These storms continued through the Quad Cities metro east towards Princeton, Sterling, and Hennepin Illinois, producing additional reports of wind damage and winds of 70 to 90 mph. Numerous power outages were also reported.

November was another month of mostly below normal rainfall across South Central Texas. Most of the northern half of the area had less than 50% of normal with some places in the northwest having less than 10%. In most of our counties the drought worsened during the month. Bandera, Comal, Gillespie, Kendall, and Kerr Counties entered Extreme (D3) Drought. Bastrop, Bexar, Blanco, Burnet, Caldwell, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Kinney, Lee, Llano, Real, Travis, Val Verde, and Williamson ended the month in Severe (D2) Drought. Uvalde and Zavala remained in D3, and Dimmit, Frio, and Maverick stayed in D2. Medina County with near normal rain actually improved from D3 to D2. Public water systems across the region had instituted some level of water restrictions. The Pecos, Frio, Nueces, Medina, and lower Guadalupe river basins reported much below normal seven-day stream flows at the end of the month. The upper and middle Guadalupe, San Antonio, Blanco, San Marcos. Brazos, and Colorado river basins reported below normal seven-day flows. Reservoirs in the drought areas were below normal with Lake Amistad 44 feet below normal. All of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect except Burnet, Kerr, and Bastrop.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge that had been dominant over the Southern Plains and Ark-La-Tex region to start the first couple of days of July had weakened by July 3rd, with a weak upper level disturbance sliding south into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. A complex of showers and thunderstorms that developed over Central and Southern Arkansas during the evening of the 2nd reinforced a weak surface trough southwest into extreme Southeast Oklahoma, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the morning hours of the 3rd, with this boundary focusing an area of compressional heating and moisture pooling throughout the day. As a result, afternoon temperatures climbed into the lower to middle 90s, with limited mixing of dewpoints resulting in oppressive heat indices of 105-110 degrees across extreme Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, extreme Northeast Texas, and Western Louisiana from late morning through the mid afternoon hours. However, showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary by early afternoon, with this complex of storms shifting west southwest across the region during the afternoon, resulting in much cooler conditions and relief to the oppressive heat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wheeler County started the month with severe drought (D2) conditions in the northern half of the county. July continued to be below normal in rainfall introducing severe drought to the entire county with some extreme drought (D3) conditions developing across the central portion of the county through the first 3 weeks of July. During the fourth week some rain fell, but it was just enough to return most of the county to severe drought with a small portion of extreme drought in the northwest corner of the county. Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracked from near Kansas City on the morning of July 15th to southern Lake Michigan by midnight on July 16th.  The low interacted with an unstable and very moist environment to produce a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) over eastern Kansas into Missouri, which then pushed into west-central Illinois by the mid to late morning of July 15th.  Several rounds of convection moved across the Illinois River Valley through the afternoon, producing heavy rain and isolated wind damage.  The heaviest rainfall of 5 to 7 inches was focused across Tazewell, Woodford, and far eastern Peoria counties where significant flash flooding occurred.  In addition, 5 weak tornadoes touched down...including 2 in Tazewell County, 1 in McLean County, 1 in Morgan County, and 1 in Montgomery County which then crossed into southern Sangamon County.  Minor damage was reported with some of the tornadoes: however, no injuries or deaths occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall of 5 to 7 inches produced widespread flash flooding across Woodford County.  Most roads were flooded in the communities of Roanoke, Panola, Eureka, Congerville, Germantown Hills, and Secor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a surface warm front that lifted slowly north across western Kentucky and southern Illinois in the afternoon. Soils were quite saturated from recent heavy rains, causing rapid runoff and isolated flash flooding. Precipitable water values ranged from 2 to 2.25 inches along the front. The heavy rain potential was limited by weak 850 mb winds around 10 knots. Strong instability contributed to a few severe storms that briefly pulsed above severe limits. Weak winds aloft limited the potential for organized strong or severe thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several inches of water flowed across Old Highway 51 near Cobden. Four other roads nearby were also covered by water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Saturday, July 11, producing widespread wind damage and very large hail. The first line of storms came through during the morning, producing damaging wind gusts and reports of quarter to ping pong ball size hail from Independence to Tipton Iowa. A wind gust of 65 MPH was measured just west of Independence. The second round of thunderstorms developed as a result of an upper level disturbance interacting with an atmosphere characterized by extremely high instability with modest vertical wind shear. Activity initially formed in north central Iowa, producing golf ball to two inch hail from Fort Dodge to Waterloo Iowa. Eventually, storms made their way towards the Cedar Rapids/Iowa City metro areas, producing widespread wind damage and hail up to baseball size. These storms continued through the Quad Cities metro east towards Princeton, Sterling, and Hennepin Illinois, producing additional reports of wind damage and winds of 70 to 90 mph. Numerous power outages were also reported.

November was another month of mostly below normal rainfall across South Central Texas. Most of the northern half of the area had less than 50% of normal with some places in the northwest having less than 10%. In most of our counties the drought worsened during the month. Bandera, Comal, Gillespie, Kendall, and Kerr Counties entered Extreme (D3) Drought. Bastrop, Bexar, Blanco, Burnet, Caldwell, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Kinney, Lee, Llano, Real, Travis, Val Verde, and Williamson ended the month in Severe (D2) Drought. Uvalde and Zavala remained in D3, and Dimmit, Frio, and Maverick stayed in D2. Medina County with near normal rain actually improved from D3 to D2. Public water systems across the region had instituted some level of water restrictions. The Pecos, Frio, Nueces, Medina, and lower Guadalupe river basins reported much below normal seven-day stream flows at the end of the month. The upper and middle Guadalupe, San Antonio, Blanco, San Marcos. Brazos, and Colorado river basins reported below normal seven-day flows. Reservoirs in the drought areas were below normal with Lake Amistad 44 feet below normal. All of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect except Burnet, Kerr, and Bastrop.

The Oswego area experienced more widespread wind damage with estimated speeds around 90 mph with isolated higher gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge of high pressure centered over the Southern Plains began to amplify and expand north-northeast into the Plains and Mississippi Valley through the middle portions of July, resulting in increased subsidence and hence, hotter temperatures as readings climbed into the mid to upper 90s across much of the Ark-La-Tex. A weak surface boundary became stationary on the 13th across portions of Northeast Texas, Southern Arkansas, and North Louisiana, which resulted in low level moisture pooling near and south of this boundary. Thus, very oppressive heat indices were observed across North-central Louisiana from the 12th-14th, with heat indices ranging from 110-115 degrees each day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms increased across eastern Oklahoma during the morning of the 28th, and the activity persisted into the afternoon. Thunderstorms redeveloped north of I-40 by mid-evening, and more thunderstorms moved into northeastern Oklahoma from southern Kansas before midnight. This activity continued to affect northeastern Oklahoma into the early afternoon of the 29th. Unseasonably rich moisture across the region for this time of year, and multiple rounds of thunderstorms affecting some of the same areas, resulted in 2-day rainfall amounts from four to nine inches across portions of Okmulgee County. This heavy rainfall caused flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roads in and around Okmulgee and Morris were flooded by heavy rainfall.

Temperatures across eastern Oklahoma in the 90s, combined with high humidity, resulted in afternoon heat indices near 110 degrees on July 1st and 2nd.

A low pressure system moving east across the central United States brought a rare summertime cold front into Louisiana on July 31st. A line of thunderstorms developed along this cold front and raced into the hot and unstable air mass ahead of the front through the day.  Damaging wind gusts accompanied these thunderstorms as they moved through northeast Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down along LA Highway 17.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of abnormally warm and dry conditions developed across portions of Deep East Texas from the final week of September through the first half of December, with rainfall amounts of near to just over two inches recorded from the 60 day period of September 24th to November 24th. This produced 60 day percentage of normal rainfall near 20 percent across portions of these areas, resulting in flash drought conditions developing by the first week of November. In fact, a small area of severe (D2) drought conditions developed by the third week of the month across the western half of Angelina and Southwestern Nacogdoches Counties on the November 19th depiction of the U.S. Drought Monitor. Periods of much needed rain did fall during the final week of the month, but this did little to improve drought conditions going into the first week of December.
