These initial thunderstorms then accelerated to the south forming a strong cold pool out ahead of the storms. Storms repeatedly formed along outflow boundaries in the central South Plains and quickly raced southward. One of these storms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter in Floyd County. This particular storm went on to produce wind damage in Ralls (Crosby County) and finally in Post (Garza County).  In far southwestern Garza County, this storm produced a wind gust to 94 mph near Graham. High precipitable water values contributed to flooding in Garza County along Texas State Highway 207 north of Post. Reports on social media showed the road had been damaged and impassable due to flooding.||Additional thunderstorms developed across the central South Plains and rushed southward from Hale into Lubbock and Lynn Counties. A large swath of severe winds initially affected a portion of Lubbock County and the city of Lubbock. The first severe wind gust was reported by the Automated Surface Observing System at Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport at 2020 CST. The Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet recorded additional severe wind gusts at Reese Center, Texas Tech University, and Slaton. These severe winds mostly affected the eastern portion of the city of Lubbock. In total, 50 power poles were downed along with a tree that fell onto and damaged a residence.||Thunderstorm outflow winds well ahead of the thunderstorms produced a severe wind gust to 58 mph at Amherst (Lamb County) at 1925 CST measured by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Silverton measured a wind gust to 72 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Employee reported a large tree, approximately two feet in diameter and 60 feet tall, down off a bike train in West Des Moines. Time estimated via radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An abnormally strong early June cold front shifted southeast across the Four State Region during the evening and overnight hours of June 9th-10th, ahead of an upper level trough of low pressure which shifted southeast through the Southern Plains and Mid/Lower Mississippi Valley. Although the atmospheric moisture profile was shallow, strong frontal forcing and moderate instability that had developed along and ahead of the front contributed to the development of a narrow line of showers and thunderstorms along the front during the early and mid-evening hours across East Texas and Southwest Arkansas, which pushed into portions of North Louisiana during the late evening and overnight hours. Some of these storms briefly became severe across East Texas, with several reports of large hail and damaging winds received. These storms did gradually weaken by late evening as they moved into South-central Arkansas and North Louisiana, given the reduced instability.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down off of FM 450 just south of Lake O' The Pines.

The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Highway 142 was flooded south of Mcleansboro in at least two spots. One car was stalled in high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire Department reported quarter sized hail mixed with smaller hail lasting approximately ten minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of a large tree branch down, reported via social media. Time estimated via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper level shortwave trough shifting northeast across Oklahoma into the Ozarks during the evening through the early morning hours of November 24th-25th, drove a surface frontal system through the Southern Plains. Large scale forcing ahead of the trough and cold front produced a line of strong thunderstorms that moved east through the Four State Region during the evening and overnight hours. Strong instability and forcing resulted in these storms exploding vigorously to the west over North Texas early in the evening, producing some severe wind gusts even as the storms moved into portions of East-central Texas, where trees were blown down in Red River, Smith, Cherokee, and Panola Counties. A brief EF-1 tornado was also spawned from these storms in Southern Panola County. These storms gradually weakened as they pushed through the remainder of East Texas into Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana,  although gusty winds of 40 to 50 mph persisted with the line of thunderstorms before weakening further just before daybreak on the 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 100 mph touched down near County Road 446 and traveled northeast for approximately a third of a mile before crossing FM 31 South near a residence. This tornado likely continued on at least a little farther downstream from this spot, but access downstream was very limited for several miles and thus the official end point of the tornado is at the crossing of FM 31 South. A few small trees were snapped at the start point of the tornado, but at FM 31 South, there were at least 10 large pine trees that were snapped or uprooted with noted signs of damage convergence. The estimated tornado path was just to the north of a residence and no real structural damage was observed.

An abnormally strong early June cold front shifted southeast across the Four State Region during the evening and overnight hours of June 9th-10th, ahead of an upper level trough of low pressure which shifted southeast through the Southern Plains and Mid/Lower Mississippi Valley. Although the atmospheric moisture profile was shallow, strong frontal forcing and moderate instability that had developed along and ahead of the front contributed to the development of a narrow line of showers and thunderstorms along the front during the early and mid-evening hours across East Texas and Southwest Arkansas, which pushed into portions of North Louisiana during the late evening and overnight hours. Some of these storms briefly became severe across East Texas, with several reports of large hail and damaging winds received. These storms did gradually weaken by late evening as they moved into South-central Arkansas and North Louisiana, given the reduced instability.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down in the Pine Harbor neighborhood near Lake O' The Pines.

The winds gusted as high as 59 mph at Wichita Eisenhower National airport, with numerous reports of tree damage in Wichita, Kansas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A plume of anomalously moist tropical air surged far northeast of Tropical Storm Cristobal, which was located over the Bay of Campeche. Numerous showers and thunderstorms redeveloped near the Martin County coast and trained across the eastern half of the county from the evening of June 2nd through the afternoon of June 3rd. High rainfall rates and excessive accumulations resulted in flood water intrusion into two dozen homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread rain totals of 5-10 inches affected portions of Jensen Beach, Stuart, Palm City and Hobe Sound between the evening of June 2 and mid afternoon on June 3. Excessive rain rates (6 inches in less than 4 hours) occurred within an area of saturated soils from Palm City to Hobe sound, with peak event total rainfall of 11 to 13 inches measured by a weatherstem site and a SKYWARN spotter, respectively, both in Hobe Sound. Fourteen homes experienced minor damage consisting of several inches of water accumulation and 8 homes sustained major damage with waters levels up to or beyond electrical outlets. Numerous roadways throughout the area became impassable due to high water and were closed. Additionally, water poured into some homes in Stuart near Manatee Pocket, where heavy rain combined with the high tide, likely causing water levels to rise along a stream connected to the St. Lucie River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rains from Tropical Depression Cristobal fell across northeast Iowa on June 9th. Rainfall amounts of 1 to 3 inches were common with locally higher totals of 4 to 5 inches. This heavy rain created flash flooding across portions of Fayette, Chickasaw and Howard Counties. Numerous roads were closed because of high water across Fayette County including State Highways 3 and 150. Roads were also closed west of Protovin (Howard County) and east of Lawler (Chickasaw County). The highest reported rainfall amounts were 5.25 inches east of Oelwein (Fayette County) and 4.6 inches west of Maynard (Fayette County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Just west of Ionia, 3.03 inches of rain fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common, and pockets of damaging wind were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several streets were briefly flooded in Perryville. Some county roads were flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: One report of quarter size hail was reported from overnight thunderstorms, which dissipated after sunrise on 6/28.

Large clusters of thunderstorms during the early morning hours produced locally excessive rainfall. The storms occurred ahead of a very compact disturbance in the upper levels of the atmosphere over areas of far west central Illinois. A shortwave trough axis extended south from the disturbance. The air mass across the region was very moist, with precipitable water values around 2 inches. There was also a pool of moderate to strong instability over central and western Missouri that advanced northeastward with the aid of a 20 to 30 kt southwest low-level jet. Torrential rainfall caused some localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous roads were flooded in West Frankfort. A rain gage near Zeigler measured 2.92 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported multiple tree limbs and power lines down in Iowa Falls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front brought a round of showers and thunderstorms to the area.  One storm produced a tornado as it moved through Madison county with some damage, resulting in damage to farm buildings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado initially touched down near NW Little Cat Road in Madison County. Significant tree damage and minor structural damage was noted at a home along County Road 150. The tree damage intensified as the tornado moved northeast across a quail farm along Boggy Bay Road. Significant tree damage and damage to farm outbuildings suggests EF-1 intensity. This was the tornado's widest point. The path narrowed as it crossed County Road 253 where a significant number of snapped pine trees was noted. The tornado then weakened, with no other known structural damage, before lifting just southwest of State Road 53 near the Florida-Georgia line. Maximum winds are estimated to be 105 mph with a maximum width of 475 yards. Thanks to Madison County Emergency Management and Florida Division of Emergency Management for help with the survey.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough was centered over southern Canada and extended southward into Texas. A dryline developed across West Texas during the afternoon with very moist air to the east of this feature. Wind shear was fairly high across the area, and there was high instability. Thunderstorms to the north of the area during the morning left a boundary in place which became a focus for thunderstorm development during the afternoon and evening hours across the Permian Basin. These conditions contributed to thunderstorms that developed across the Permian Basin and in Brewster County that produced large hail and strong winds.

The upper level winds were from the northwest and an upper level disturbance moved southeastward on the upper winds. This resulted in thunderstorms that developed in the higher terrain of northeast New Mexico. These thunderstorms organized into a complex of thunderstorms known as an MCS (Mesoscale Convective System). Behind this complex of thunderstorms was a cold front. The air across the Permian Basin was moist and unstable.This complex of storms moved into the Permian Basin during the late evening and overnight hours and produced hail and strong, damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm moved across Scurry County and produced a 72 mph wind gust at the mesonet site near Snyder. A 100 foot radio tower in Snyder was blown over due to the winds. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was draped from the Carolina's through the northeastern Bahamas, with a zone of deeper moistures situated across South Florida. Prevailing east-southeasterly flow allowed for both the Gulf Atlantic sea breeze to progress inland through peak heating hours. Several pockets of cooler, drier air aloft worked in concert with steepening low-level lapses to produce sufficient accent for showers and thunderstorms to develop within the saturated airmass. Collisions between the sea breeze boundaries and additional outflow boundaries resulted in a few stronger storms that produced a funnel cloud and flooding across Palm Beach.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spotter reported a funnel cloud extending 80 percent of the way to the ground from cloud base in the Belle Glade area. Spotter noted that the funnel did not extend to the ground. This was associated with generating convection that interacted with a lake-breeze boundary peripheral to Lake Okeechobee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported a six inch tree branch down. Time estimated via radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Large clusters of thunderstorms during the early morning hours produced locally excessive rainfall. The storms occurred ahead of a very compact disturbance in the upper levels of the atmosphere over areas of far west central Illinois. A shortwave trough axis extended south from the disturbance. The air mass across the region was very moist, with precipitable water values around 2 inches. There was also a pool of moderate to strong instability over central and western Missouri that advanced northeastward with the aid of a 20 to 30 kt southwest low-level jet. Torrential rainfall caused some localized flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two mesoscale cycloncic vortex systems (MCVs) produced several severe thunderstorms across the area from early morning through the mid afternoon hours of Wednesday June 24, 2020. There were several tornadoes reported with these severe thunderstorms as they moved across the area. The most significant tornadoes impacted the Baton Rouge area, the Salem area of Walthall County, and the Mississippi Gulf Coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service Damage Assessment Team has surveyed the storm damage in Baton Rouge, LA. It has been determined the damage was the result of a tornado. The tornado has been rated an EF-1 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. Damage estimates were consistent with winds of 110 mph.||The tornado first touched down near Essen Park Avenue, just south of the Interstate 10 near Essen Lane.  It produced minor roof damage to the Fairfield Inn, snapped a few smaller trees and knocked down a light pole.  The tornado rapidly intensified, producing significantly more damage just moments later.  As the tornado reached two Ammon Staffing buildings, it downed fencing, peeled the northern side metal roof of, and blew out a window on the east side of the building.  Of the two buildings, the western one was damaged the most.  More than half its flat roof was ripped off or collapsed.   There was a partial collapse of the southwest exterior wall on the second story.  It is suspected that a large limb or some other object hit that corner of the building, which could have aided in the lifting of the roof.  No roof straps were seen during the survey.  The tornado also damaged the roof of a building just to the east of the Ammon Staffing Buildings.  Only the center section of the roof was removed and the rafters actually remained intact.  Based on the overall damage of these 3 buildings, a peak wind speed of 110 mph was given at this point which was the strongest point of the tornado's track.  These winds carried over into those building's parking lot to carry debris and, based on tire slide marks, may have pushed a vehicle through a chain link fence to the interstate on-ramp. ||The tornado the crossed Interstate 10.  On the north side of the interstate, it downed smaller trees, ripped off some vinyl siding and damaged the roof slightly.  The tornado continued northeastward, downing several large trees and powerlines along Essen Heights Ct. The tornado then moved through Westminster, downing multiple trees across several streets.  As the tornado passed over Westminster Elementary School, it damaged the school sign and ripped skirting of modular classrooms.  The strength of the tornado would generally only weaken from this point onward.  Tree damage persisted along a path through the I-12 and Airline Highway intersection.  Minor commercial building window damage was noted near the Costco.  The last few points of damage were just east-northeast of this location through Cedarcrest Avenue and finally Old Hammond Highway just east of Sherwood Blvd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported downed large tree branches and trees at relative's home. Garage and power lines damaged by downed trees. Time estimated via radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions remained relatively steady through the month. Both Briscoe and Motley Counties showed slight improvement while Crosby County worsened. Exceptional drought (D4) to extreme drought (D3) conditions remained over much of the South Plains and extended into portions of the Rolling Plains and Childress County. Most of the Rolling Plains remained in abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought (D1).||Only one notable precipitation event occurred during the month of November. A significant amount of rainfall was observed in Stonewall County where Aspermont received 1.50 inches of rainfall. However, areas on the Caprock received significantly less rainfall with values on the order of up to one quarter inch. Soil moisture outside of areas with irrigation remains very low, especially on the Caprock where the soil moisture ranks in the lowest first percentile. Cattle continued to require supplemental feed amid poor pasture conditions on the South Plains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front by mid-late afternoon across central Kentucky, moving into eastern Kentucky during the late afternoon and evening hours. Initially, many of these storms contained strong enough outflow winds to produce damage to trees as well as a couple of structures. As these storms moved farther east of U.S. Highway 23 into the mid evening hours closer to sunset, they weakened below severe limits. Additionally, stronger upper level forcing across northern to central Kentucky versus southern Kentucky helped to spare southeast Kentucky from any damaging winds.||As the cold front moved through during the late evening hours to just after midnight, strong winds accompanied the frontal passage across isolated portions of Floyd and Pike Counties.

The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal lifted north across Central and Eastern Louisiana during the daytime hours of June 8th after making landfall along the Southern Louisiana coast during the evening hours of the 7th. Scattered showers and a few isolated thunderstorms developed throughout the afternoon and rotated west southwest around the center of circulation as it entered extreme Southern Arkansas during the late afternoon hours. Precipitation loading resulted in isolated instances of damaging winds across Bowie County Texas, where several trees were snapped or had fallen on homes in Dekalb, power lines were downed, and the metal roof of a large storage barn was peeled back.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Damaging winds snapped several trees and power lines in Dekalb. A tree was blown down onto a home in town, with others down across roadways. The metal roof of a large barn was peeled back.

These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.

The tornado has been rated an EF-0 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. Damage estimates were consistent with winds of 85 mph.||The tornado touched down just west of Bueche Rd, tearing some siding of of a house.  In addition, the roof of a garage building was damaged from trees.  It also uprooted trees and snapped tree limbs as it progressed in an eastward direction.  It lifted on Bueche Rd. just short o Clause Bayou.  It is possible that the tornado started and ended before and after the stated locations, but these areas were inaccessible or were surrounded by fields.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estherville ASOS report of 60 mph wind gust.

The quick exit of Cristobal was due in part to a strong shortwave moving across the northern plains that helped to kick Cristobal from the area. This secondary system moved into Iowa the evening of June 9th, and while for the most part remained sub-severe, damaging winds were reported in west-central Iowa with a stronger cell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coop observer recorded 2.57 inches of rainfall over the last 24 hours.

Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front by mid-late afternoon across central Kentucky, moving into eastern Kentucky during the late afternoon and evening hours. Initially, many of these storms contained strong enough outflow winds to produce damage to trees as well as a couple of structures. As these storms moved farther east of U.S. Highway 23 into the mid evening hours closer to sunset, they weakened below severe limits. Additionally, stronger upper level forcing across northern to central Kentucky versus southern Kentucky helped to spare southeast Kentucky from any damaging winds.||As the cold front moved through during the late evening hours to just after midnight, strong winds accompanied the frontal passage across isolated portions of Floyd and Pike Counties.

A series of heavy rainfall events in mid and late May caused the Mississippi River to rise back above flood stage. The flooding was minor, consisting of flooded fields, low-lying access roads, and some riverside parkland. Some minor crop damage likely occurred. The river fell back below flood stage in mid June.

A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mason City ASOS recorded gust of 54 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure draped across the region brought east to southeasterly flow. This pattern favors the development of both The Atlantic and Gulf sea breezes each afternoon. Additionally, a plume of Saharan dust was slowly trickling in from the Caribbean, bringing drier air to the midlevels, while the leading edge also acted as a pseudo elevated mixed layer, enhancing updraft strength enough to produce hail in a few stronger storms over Glades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Brighton Reservation Police reported Nickel size hail (0.88 inches) and wind gusts up to 50 mph with storms over the Cane Hill area of the reservation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Afternoon convection initiated along the Atlantic and Gulf sea breezes as these boundaries pushed inland. Despite the presence of the Saharan Air Layer (SAL) over the region, several perturbations from the Bahamas allowed for an uptick in convective coverage as they moved across the area. The leading edge of SAL allowed for a few stronger storms to develop and produced hail across Broward and Palm Beach.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spotter reported hail between dime and nickel size from a strong thunderstorm about 1 mile NW from the intersection of Weston Road and Griffin Road. Pea size hailed was also reported by the public via social media near Emerald Estates.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A northward retreating frontal boundary allowed for generally east to southeasterly flow to keep abundant moisture in place across South Florida. Morning thunderstorms developed over Miami-Dade, with lightning striking a home, causing some damage. Thankfully no one was injured.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An article from Local 10 News reported a house near the intersection of Bryon Ave and 92nd Street was struck by lightning from a thunderstorm that pushed across the town of Surfside in the morning.  Lightning struck a tall structure on the roof, blowing up the concrete, which landed in six or seven different places and even hit his SUV, though it only caused a few scratches. Thankfully, no one was injured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South-southwesterly flow allowed for deep tropical moisture to stay in place across South Florida. This prevailing flow also allowed the Gulf sea breeze to progress further inland, pinning the Atlantic sea breeze to the coast, becoming the focus for afternoon showers and thunderstorm. As a mid-upper level shortwave rotated across the region aloft through the day, coverage of thunderstorms increased along the east coast and brought gusty winds and heavy rainfall that lead to flash flooding in Broward and Palm Beach.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media relayed public reports of wind damage to homes and trees in the West Boca area. Several patios lost their roofs and large tree limbs were also downed. Wind gust estimated from a mesonet station east of the damage area at approximately 56 mph (47kt). Time also estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager report of 60 mph wind gust.

Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front by mid-late afternoon across central Kentucky, moving into eastern Kentucky during the late afternoon and evening hours. Initially, many of these storms contained strong enough outflow winds to produce damage to trees as well as a couple of structures. As these storms moved farther east of U.S. Highway 23 into the mid evening hours closer to sunset, they weakened below severe limits. Additionally, stronger upper level forcing across northern to central Kentucky versus southern Kentucky helped to spare southeast Kentucky from any damaging winds.||As the cold front moved through during the late evening hours to just after midnight, strong winds accompanied the frontal passage across isolated portions of Floyd and Pike Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter and dispatch reported trees downed along Kentucky Highway 39 between Woodstock and Bandy. Near Bandy, Kentucky Highway 70 had a tree downed near it while another tree was blown down onto a trailer with a barn being knocked down as well.

A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 60 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tight pressure gradient between a subtropical high in the Atlantic and Tropical Depression Cristobal over the Yucatan Peninsula helped to loft deep tropical moisture into South Florida. An outflow boundary racing northward from Cuba and strengthening southwesterly flow in the upper levels in association with an upper-level trough over the northern Gulf of Mexico provided sufficient lift and enough synoptic ascent for thunderstorms to develop in the afternoon and evening hours. With the abundant moisture in place, flash flooding occurred across Palm Beach. A Flood Watch was in Effect through 8PM EDT June 6.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports from the Town of Jupiter Police Dispatch of blocked, impassable streets and vehicles stranded in the 400 block of Hugh street and Near the Jupiter River Estates neighborhood. Social media posts by WPTV and CBS 12 in Palm Beach also showed half-foot of water on SR 811/Alt A1A in Jupiter and water completely covering Pittsburgh Drive in Jupiter, with water reaching about halfway up front yards. A total of 3 to 4 inches fell in that area, most of it in about an hour's time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter estimated winds of 60 to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: By the morning of June 9 remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal pushed north into Iowa, drenching central and eastern Iowa for most of the day before lifting into the Great Lakes region by evening. The quick exit of Cristobal was due in part to a strong shortwave moving across the northern plains that helped to kick Cristobal from the area. This secondary system moved into Iowa the evening of June 9th, and while for the most part remained sub-severe, damaging winds were reported in west-central Iowa with a stronger cell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coop observer recorded 3.25 inches of rainfall over the last 24 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unusual warmth with a week of temperatures mainly in the 70s (even 50s and 60s on November 9 less than a day before this storm) was brought to an abrupt end as a deep trough of low pressure moved out of Rockies and into the Plains.  An intense lower- to mid-level frontal zone oozed eastward as a strong jet lifted out across the Plains on November 10, initiating widespread precipitation.  More rapid shallow cooling occurred across northwest Iowa and led to a swath of freezing rain which accumulated from a tenth to a half inch during the overnight and morning hours, before changing to snow in the afternoon.  Heavier and more persistent snowfall occurred with the deeper cooling to the northwest across southeast South Dakota, far northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota, where amounts ranged from 3 to 7 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow was intermittently mixed with light freezing rain during the morning with up to a tenth of an inch ice accumulation. Snow continued through afternoon, and was briefly heavy between 1300-1600CST. Snowfall totaled 6.5 inches at Sibley.

A compact upper level closed low quickly moved across eastern New Mexico and West Texas on the morning of the 28th. Temperatures dropped enough during the early morning hours for rain to change to all snow in Parmer County.  A cooperative weather observer in Friona measured 1.0 inches of snow.

A vigorous upper level shortwave trough shifting northeast across Oklahoma into the Ozarks during the evening through the early morning hours of November 24th-25th, drove a surface frontal system through the Southern Plains. Large scale forcing ahead of the trough and cold front produced a line of strong thunderstorms that moved east through the Four State Region during the evening and overnight hours. Strong instability and forcing resulted in these storms exploding vigorously to the west over North Texas early in the evening, producing some severe wind gusts even as the storms moved into portions of East-central Texas, where trees were blown down in Red River, Smith, Cherokee, and Panola Counties. A brief EF-1 tornado was also spawned from these storms in Southern Panola County. These storms gradually weakened as they pushed through the remainder of East Texas into Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana,  although gusty winds of 40 to 50 mph persisted with the line of thunderstorms before weakening further just before daybreak on the 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown over Highway 37 and FM 2120 north of Clarksville. Lots of tree debris was also found over Highway 37.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common, and an isolated damaging microburst occurred.

Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level longwave trough emerged out of the Intermountain West and into the Central and Southern Plains during the daytime and evening hours of January 10th. A strong southerly return flow commenced out ahead of the trough during the 8th-9th, allowing for unseasonably warm and humid conditions to advance northward across Southern Oklahoma, much of Central and Eastern Texas, as well as Louisiana, Arkansas, and the Lower Mississippi Valley. Meanwhile, an intensifying surface low pressure system and associated dry line developed along the Red River of North Texas into Southern Oklahoma during the afternoon hours, which spread east northeast across the Ark-La-Tex during the early morning hours on January 11th. With afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 70s ahead of this trough, moderate instability developed across the broad warm sector, with very strong wind shear in place as large scale forcing increased ahead of the trough axis across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. Thus, an axis of strong to severe showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours across Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas and East Texas, which advanced east into North Louisiana during the early morning hours of the 11th. Damaging winds downed trees and power lines across portions of East Texas, with even multiple tornadoes touching down along the line of severe thunderstorms. Unfortunately, a man  was killed when a tornado touched down west of Nacogdoches and a tree fell on his mobile home. These storms also produced locally heavy rainfall, with amounts of one to three inches, with isolated higher amounts up to four inches recorded across much of this area, resulting in isolated instances of flash flooding. These storms continued to intensify during the late evening and early morning hours as they moved into extreme Eastern Texas and Western Louisiana, producing more in the way of widespread wind damage and isolated tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down across Farm to Market Road 225 south of Henderson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tight pressure gradient between a subtropical high in the Atlantic and Tropical Depression Cristobal over the Yucatan Peninsula helped to loft deep tropical moisture into South Florida. An outflow boundary racing northward from Cuba and strengthening southwesterly flow in the upper levels in association with an upper-level trough over the northern Gulf of Mexico provided sufficient lift and enough synoptic ascent for thunderstorms to develop in the afternoon and evening hours. With the abundant moisture in place, flash flooding occurred across Palm Beach. A Flood Watch was in Effect through 8PM EDT June 6.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tequesta Police Department reported numerous streets flooded in the town from significant flooding. Streets included: Old Dixie Highway, Country Club Drive, Fairway West, Riverside Drive, and Yacht Club Place. Water was between waist and knee high in these areas. Several vehicles had to be towed/pushed from deep water. Over 4 inches of rain was measured by nearby gauges, with hourly rates of over 3 inches per hour.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS employee reported winds of 60 mph.

The quick exit of Cristobal was due in part to a strong shortwave moving across the northern plains that helped to kick Cristobal from the area. This secondary system moved into Iowa the evening of June 9th, and while for the most part remained sub-severe, damaging winds were reported in west-central Iowa with a stronger cell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper level shortwave trough shifting northeast across Oklahoma into the Ozarks during the evening through the early morning hours of November 24th-25th, drove a surface frontal system through the Southern Plains. Large scale forcing ahead of the trough and cold front produced a line of strong thunderstorms that moved east through the Four State Region during the evening and overnight hours. Strong instability and forcing resulted in these storms exploding vigorously to the west over North Texas early in the evening, producing some severe wind gusts even as the storms moved into portions of East-central Texas. These storms gradually weakened as they pushed through the remainder of East Texas, but strengthened as they moved into Northwest Louisiana (including Shreveport) after 2 am, where 60 mph winds were measured and downed trees and power lines across portions of Caddo, Bossier, Webster, and Bienville Parishes. These storms weakened further just before daybreak on the 25th as they moved across Northcentral Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 mph wind gust was measured at the Shreveport Regional Airport.

Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front by mid-late afternoon across central Kentucky, moving into eastern Kentucky during the late afternoon and evening hours. Initially, many of these storms contained strong enough outflow winds to produce damage to trees as well as a couple of structures. As these storms moved farther east of U.S. Highway 23 into the mid evening hours closer to sunset, they weakened below severe limits. Additionally, stronger upper level forcing across northern to central Kentucky versus southern Kentucky helped to spare southeast Kentucky from any damaging winds.||As the cold front moved through during the late evening hours to just after midnight, strong winds accompanied the frontal passage across isolated portions of Floyd and Pike Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet reported a tree downed along Kentucky Highway 89 near Foxtown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed over Southeast Texas during the mid and late afternoon hours, along the tail end of an upper trough axis that extended from Western Arkansas across Western Louisiana and extreme Eastern Texas. Afternoon temperatures in the lower 90s within the moist air mass contributed to moderate instability developing as these storms shifted north-northeast, with an isolated severe thunderstorm developing as it moved along the Cherokee/Angelina County Texas line. This storm produced damaging winds which downed power lines just southeast of Wells before quickly weakening as it moved into Southwest Nacogdoches County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were downed on County Road 2 just southeast of Wells.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common, and an isolated damaging microburst occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Six utility poles were broken on the west side of Paducah.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A training thunderstorm complex during the night of June 27th into the 28th produced significant flash flooding, as well as minor river flooding on the Green River. The maximum axis of rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches occurred over portions of northwest Kentucky, just south of the cities of Owensboro and Henderson. A weak mid-level disturbance advanced east early in the morning across eastern IL. This energy helped foster thunderstorm activity across portions of southern IL, southern IN, and Kentucky. The air mass around the southern flank of the disturbance was still at least modestly unstable with mixed layer capes around 1000 j/kg early in the morning. A west-southwest low-level wind flow between 30 and 40 knots focused strong moisture transport into the storms. The storms trained over the same area for three to five hours. Precipitable water values across the region were on the order of 1.7 to 1.9 inches, fueling rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust to 65 mph was measured at the Kentucky mesonet site in Todd County. A nearby carport structure was blown over.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low pressure system brought periods of cool weather with windy and rainy conditions to Southern California. Gusty winds in excess of 60 MPH were reported along with some light precipitation of up to a half inch from the coast to the mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gusty westerly winds occurred, highest near the foothills of the San Bernardino Mountains. Winds 40-50 MPH reported, some sites as high as 67 MPH at Whitewater.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge across much of the midwest brought the first round of summer-like temperatures to the area in early June. By late in the day a shortwave moving across the northern plains flattened the nose of the ridge a pulled a cool front across northern Iowa. Convection developed along this boundary in the evening in the form of gusty winds across northern Iowa. Convection then diminished overnight as the front continued to sink south across the state. By early morning the front had made it to central Iowa where storms restrengthened, dropping large hail and producing gusty winds. By mid-morning the front had pushed south of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of golf ball sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station reported a 24 hour rain total of of 2.20 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level longwave trough emerged out of the Intermountain West and into the Central and Southern Plains during the daytime and evening hours of January 10th. A strong southerly return flow commenced out ahead of the trough during the 8th-9th, allowing for unseasonably warm and humid conditions to advance northward across Southern Oklahoma, much of Central and Eastern Texas, as well as Louisiana, Arkansas, and the Lower Mississippi Valley. Meanwhile, an intensifying surface low pressure system and associated dry line developed along the Red River of North Texas into Southern Oklahoma during the afternoon hours, which spread east northeast across the Ark-La-Tex during the early morning hours on January 11th. With afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 70s ahead of this trough, moderate instability developed across the broad warm sector, with very strong wind shear in place as large scale forcing increased ahead of the trough axis across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. Thus, an axis of strong to severe showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours across Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas and East Texas, which advanced east into North Louisiana during the early morning hours of the 11th. Damaging winds downed trees and power lines across portions of East Texas, with even multiple tornadoes touching down along the line of severe thunderstorms. Unfortunately, a man  was killed when a tornado touched down west of Nacogdoches and a tree fell on his mobile home. These storms also produced locally heavy rainfall, with amounts of one to three inches, with isolated higher amounts up to four inches recorded across much of this area, resulting in isolated instances of flash flooding. These storms continued to intensify during the late evening and early morning hours as they moved into extreme Eastern Texas and Western Louisiana, producing more in the way of widespread wind damage and isolated tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed at the intersection of Highway 42 and Highway 323 near New London.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was draped from the Carolina's through the northeastern Bahamas, with a zone of deeper moistures situated across South Florida. Prevailing east-southeasterly flow allowed for both the Gulf Atlantic sea breeze to progress inland through peak heating hours. Several pockets of cooler, drier air aloft worked in concert with steepening low-level lapses to produce sufficient accent for showers and thunderstorms to develop within the saturated airmass. Collisions between the sea breeze boundaries and additional outflow boundaries resulted in a few stronger storms that produced a funnel cloud and flooding across Palm Beach.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snap map image of poor-drainage-related flooding of residential property in the Belle Glade area, enhanced by runoff from earlier heavy rains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Modest easterly flow helped to keep the Gulf Breeze pinned along the coast. Afternoon showers and thunderstorms developed as the Atlantic breeze moved inland and collided with the Gulf Breeze. A mid level trough situated along the the west coast and abundant moisture in place aided in producing robust updrafts that allowed several rounds of heavy rainfall producing thunderstorms over Naples, which resulted in Flash Flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports from the public and social media of widespread street flooding in downtown Naples near the intersection of south 9th street and south 5th avenue through West Lake in Downtown Naples, where a sports utility vehicle was largely submerged into a storm-drain runoff area. The significant flooding extended northward along North Tamiami Trail, North of Naples Bay, where water was seen extending over street surfaces onto sidewalks and continuing across Quail Run Golf Club in Naples just south of Pine Ridge Road, where a few cars were flooded by becoming partially submerged in flood waters. Areas of flooding extended a couple feet deep over streets and surrounding property. A report from an automated rain gauge within Wunderground Network -- Site ID KFLNAPLE256, which is located near the intersection of Leeward Lane and Putter Point Drive recorded a total of 4.7 inches of rain that fell in association with heavy showers and thunderstorms over several hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS reported a 24 hour rain total of 2.04 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between 9 p.m. and midnight CDT on this Wednesday evening, a smattering of mostly-weak thunderstorms rumbled from west-to-east across portions of this six-county North Central Kansas area, as the vast majority of severe storms in the region focused at least slightly off to the north and east. However, between 10:30-11:15 p.m. CDT, one small storm cluster flared up to severe levels over Jewell County, yielding a lone ground-truth report of measured 68 MPH winds in the far northeast corner of the county near Webber. Radar also indicated that this storm might have produced severe-criteria hail over mainly central sections of the county, but there were no verifying reports. In the mid-upper levels, this was not a strongly-forced event, with the main feature consisting of a low-amplitude shortwave trough tracking east-southeast across Nebraska out of western SD over the course of the afternoon-evening. Surface features in North Central Kansas during the evening were fairly nondescript, dominated by weak high pressure and generally southerly breezes around 10 MPH or less. However, fairly steep low-mid level lapse rates were in place, as evening mesoscale analysis revealed around 2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 35 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Well above normal levels of tropical moisture over Martin County allowed an area of heavy showers and thunderstorms to develop during the afternoon and move slowly across an area saturated from excessive rain which fell over previous days. Flooding quickly redeveloped, with water entering into several homes, mainly in the town of Hobe Sound.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two to four inches of rain fell within two hours, across an area which received 7 to 13 inches of rain over the previous three days. With saturated soils and standing water remaining in many areas, flooding quickly developed. Flood waters entered several homes, mainly within Hobe Heights. Some homes may have experienced water intrusion two days earlier from the first period of flooding. Numerous roadways within Hobe Sound became inpassable due to high levels of standing water.

Additional damage occurred on Bristol Circle and Ashley Court where several fences were blow over, small trees toppled, medium tree branches downed, and loose backyard items tossed into adjacent properties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common, and pockets of damaging wind were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Six-inch tree branches were broken off.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A training thunderstorm complex during the night of June 27th into the 28th produced significant flash flooding, as well as minor river flooding on the Green River. The maximum axis of rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches occurred over portions of northwest Kentucky, just south of the cities of Owensboro and Henderson. A weak mid-level disturbance advanced east early in the morning across eastern IL. This energy helped foster thunderstorm activity across portions of southern IL, southern IN, and Kentucky. The air mass around the southern flank of the disturbance was still at least modestly unstable with mixed layer capes around 1000 j/kg early in the morning. A west-southwest low-level wind flow between 30 and 40 knots focused strong moisture transport into the storms. The storms trained over the same area for three to five hours. Precipitable water values across the region were on the order of 1.7 to 1.9 inches, fueling rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding of roads became rather widespread. Some roads were impassable. Water rescues were conducted from vehicles that were stranded in floodwaters. Rainfall amounts were heaviest in southeast parts of the county, where close to 8 inches fell in a 48-hour period. Much of that rain fell early on the 28th. A trained spotter just east of Corydon measured 7.85 inches during the daytime hours on the 28th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge across much of the midwest brought the first round of summer-like temperatures to the area in early June. By late in the day a shortwave moving across the northern plains flattened the nose of the ridge a pulled a cool front across northern Iowa. Convection developed along this boundary in the evening in the form of gusty winds across northern Iowa. Convection then diminished overnight as the front continued to sink south across the state. By early morning the front had made it to central Iowa where storms restrengthened, dropping large hail and producing gusty winds. By mid-morning the front had pushed south of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of nickle sized hail.

This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.

This secondary system moved into Iowa the evening of June 9th, and while for the most part remained sub-severe, damaging winds were reported in west-central Iowa with a stronger cell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public weather station measured 2.1 inches of rain. Beginning time estimated by radar. Rain ongoing at observation time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Conditions became favorable for severe weather in central Florida due to enhanced winds aloft on the far eastern periphery of Tropical Storm Cristobal which was moving north over the central Gulf of Mexico. Scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed across Lake, Orange and Volusia counties producing areas of damaging winds and several tornadoes and waterspouts over inland lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous eyewitness reports, photographs and video were received from trained spotters and the public of a large waterspout that developed on Lake Monroe, which then came onshore briefly along the north shore of the lake as a rapidly weakening tornado. The waterspout developed on Lake Monroe at approximately 1927 LST and quickly became large, reaching an estimated maximum width of approximately 200 yards. The slow-moving waterspout then reached the north side of the lake near the 860th block of Lakeshore Drive in Enterprise at approximately 1934 LST as a rapidly weakening EF-0 tornado. The tornado dissipated between Lakeshore Drive and Jacob Brock Avenue, just east of the Florida United Methodist Children's Home and west of Broadway Street. An eyewitness near the point of dissipation, initially observed the waterspout over the lake, then described a complete lull of wind, followed by a increase of winds from the opposite direction, suddenly becoming very strong. Based on this report, along with only minor damage to trees near the lakefront, peak winds were estimated between 45 and 55 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common, and pockets of damaging wind were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple of classrooms were flooded at a church in Miner.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent thunderstorms produced flash flooding in the Owensboro area. A mid-level circulation over southeast Missouri helped to focus shower and thunderstorm activity into southern Illinois and northwest Kentucky.  This circulation was associated with a trough from 850-700 mb.  Out ahead of the trough, the air mass was quite unstable with mixed layer capes approaching 2000 j/kg. Precipitable water values in the axis of instability increased to near 2 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding of numerous roads occurred in the city of Owensboro. Several roads were impassable for an extended period of time in the city and in rural locations west and southwest of the city. Vehicles were stranded in some locations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A training thunderstorm complex during the night of June 27th into the 28th produced significant flash flooding, as well as minor river flooding on the Green River. The maximum axis of rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches occurred over portions of northwest Kentucky, just south of the cities of Owensboro and Henderson. A weak mid-level disturbance advanced east early in the morning across eastern IL. This energy helped foster thunderstorm activity across portions of southern IL, southern IN, and Kentucky. The air mass around the southern flank of the disturbance was still at least modestly unstable with mixed layer capes around 1000 j/kg early in the morning. A west-southwest low-level wind flow between 30 and 40 knots focused strong moisture transport into the storms. The storms trained over the same area for three to five hours. Precipitable water values across the region were on the order of 1.7 to 1.9 inches, fueling rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous water rescues were conducted due to vehicles in floodwaters across the county, including the city of Owensboro. A trained spotter at Utica measured 5.34 inches by mid-morning, with rain still falling.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge across much of the midwest brought the first round of summer-like temperatures to the area in early June. By late in the day a shortwave moving across the northern plains flattened the nose of the ridge a pulled a cool front across northern Iowa. Convection developed along this boundary in the evening in the form of gusty winds across northern Iowa. Convection then diminished overnight as the front continued to sink south across the state. By early morning the front had made it to central Iowa where storms restrengthened, dropping large hail and producing gusty winds. By mid-morning the front had pushed south of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong gusts of 66 mph reported at Estherville Airport ASOS well in advance of approaching thunderstorms.

These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of golf ball sized hail.

This secondary system moved into Iowa the evening of June 9th, and while for the most part remained sub-severe, damaging winds were reported in west-central Iowa with a stronger cell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Conditions became favorable for severe weather in central Florida due to enhanced winds aloft on the far eastern periphery of Tropical Storm Cristobal which was moving north over the central Gulf of Mexico. The waterspout then moved back onshore as a tornado at the south end of Ferncreek Avenue. The tornado nearly paralleled Ferncreek Avenue and Martin Street as it moved nearly due north, crossing State Road 408, and lifting at Lake Lawsona Park at approximately 1832LST.||Damage was continuous along a 5.1 mile swath with a width of 350-500 yards. As the tornado came onshore at Hoffner Avenue it briefly attained EF-1 intensity (peak winds estimated at 85-90 mph) resulting in severe damage to the roof of a lakefront home and numerous large trees were toppled. Damage along much of the remainder of the path was rated EF-0 (winds estimated 65-85 mph).||The EF-0 damage consisted generally of uprooted trees, toppled trees, and snapped large branches. Several large trees fell onto homes, causing significant damage mainly to roofs. Multiple vehicles were damaged due to downed trees and fallen large branches. ||The tornado reached peak intensity of EF-1 in the vicinity of Ferncreek Avenue, Lake Margaret Drive and Carmia Drive (estimated peak winds 100-105 mph). EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A training thunderstorm complex during the night of June 27th into the 28th produced significant flash flooding, as well as minor river flooding on the Green River. The maximum axis of rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches occurred over portions of northwest Kentucky, just south of the cities of Owensboro and Henderson. A weak mid-level disturbance advanced east early in the morning across eastern IL. This energy helped foster thunderstorm activity across portions of southern IL, southern IN, and Kentucky. The air mass around the southern flank of the disturbance was still at least modestly unstable with mixed layer capes around 1000 j/kg early in the morning. A west-southwest low-level wind flow between 30 and 40 knots focused strong moisture transport into the storms. The storms trained over the same area for three to five hours. Precipitable water values across the region were on the order of 1.7 to 1.9 inches, fueling rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minor flooding of the Green River inundated low-lying woods, fields, and some croplands. The flooding continued into July.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several upper level disturbances passed over the frontal zone and interacted with increasing low level moisture to produce several rounds of moderate to heavy rainfall from the evening of the 20th to the pre-dawn hours of the 22nd. Rainfall accumulations for the 48-hour period ending at 3 AM on the 22nd ranged from one to two inches, with the highest totals over the eastern Ozarks. Localized flooding of low water crossings over southwest and south central Missouri led to two fatalities during the early morning of the 22nd. The first fatality occurred in Wright County at AB Highway north of Mansfield along Wolf Creek. An 18-year old female drove into the flooded low water crossing at around 12:30 AM, and drowned while trying to escape her vehicle. The second fatality occurred in Dent County around 5 AM. A driver with a six-year old passenger drove into the flooded low water crossing on Highway TT at Crooked Creek northeast of Salem. The driver was able to swim to safety, but the 6-year old was swept downstream and drowned.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Roubidoux Creek reached minor flood stage causing water to impact Highway 17 in northern Texas County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South-southwesterly flow allowed for deep tropical moisture to stay in place across South Florida. This prevailing flow also allowed the Gulf sea breeze to progress further inland, pinning the Atlantic sea breeze to the coast, becoming the focus for afternoon showers and thunderstorm. As a mid-upper level shortwave rotated across the region aloft through the day, coverage of thunderstorms increased along the east coast and brought gusty winds and heavy rainfall that lead to flash flooding in Broward and Palm Beach.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media relayed a public report of a large downed oak tree on Del Prado Circle in West Boca. Wind gust estimated from a mesonet station east of the damage area at approximately 56 mph (47kt). Time was also estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Light east to southeasterly flow around the Atlantic Ridge allowed for both sea breeze circulations to develop in the afternoon. Despite ridging present aloft, ample low level moisture was in place for convection to initiate along the aforementioned boundaries. A few storms were able to become strong with the leading edge of the Saharan Air Layer (SAL) approaching the region, which acted as an elevated mixed layer. One of the stronger storms produced a funnel cloud along a boundary collision over Palm Beach.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Off-duty NWS employee observed a funnel cloud -- possibly a pair of funnel clouds -- looking southeastward from the intersection of Florida Highway 700 and Everglades Street in Canal Point. The off-duty NWS employee observed the eastern funnel quickly elongate and assume a rope-type appearance before dissipating concurrent with the expansion of the peripheral rain shaft -- all while observing the visible cloud rotation and funnel base remaining well elevated above ground. A sheriff officer from South Bay also reported hail around half an inch and wind gusts around 50 mph along US 27 at Okeelanta associated with these storms.

This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep tropical moisture was in place (PWAT 2.5) with the area on the east side of TS |Cristobal as the storm approached the LA Gulf Coast. Waves of moderate to heavy rainfall with isolated embedded thunderstorms pivoted northward across the local forecast area into the evening with a more solid band of moderate to heavy rainfall developing across north Florida as low level convergence increased between a lifting frontal zones across south-central  FL and a persistent low level ridge axis holding firm just north of the Altamaha River basin. This ridge will limit the northward extend/expansion of the convective band into Sun, and generally focused a W-E oriented swath of heavy rainfall generally near and south of the I-10 corridor overnight into Sunday morning on 6/7.  The ridge strengthened north of the Altamaha Region Sun afternoon 6/7, which shunt the corridor of heavy rain SSW toward the I-75 corridor of NE FL with drier mid level air (700-500 mb) decreasing rain chances across SE GA and eastern NE FL into Sun evening. In addition to heavy rainfall potential, there was a low tornado threat for NE FL into the evening of 6/6 with elevated 0-1 km shear values 20-25 kts with low level ESE winds under increasing  SSW winds out of the GOMEX, with speeds increasing to 35-45 kts at 850 mb through 06z Sun 6/7.
