EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous winter system impacted the area, resulting in rapidly falling temperatures with the cold front passage, strong winds statewide regularly gusting to or over 50 mph, and blizzard conditions in northwest Iowa where snow accumulation was greatest. Synoptically, two areas of low pressure merged across northern Iowa and lifted northeast, pulling a cold front across the area. Precipitation developed along the initial cold front, though better moisture and additional snow fell within the deformation zone of the system. Winds remained elevated during this time, resulting in widespread diminished visibility across northern Iowa much of the afternoon and evening.

A winter storm dumped heavy snow from Roscoe south to Sterling City, Barnhart and Ozona.  This storm also produced a mixture of freezing rain, sleet and snow over the remainder of West Central Texas.  The freezing rain that fell before the snow was heavy enough to result in scattered tree limb damage and power outages across the area.  However, Coleman County was hardest hit by the ice that left many without power.  Most of the snow ended south of Interstate 20 before midnight, but some of the snow continued into New Years Day mainly along and north of Interstate 20.  The ice and snow also made travel difficult across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell across the western portions and the higher elevations of Tom Green County.  Water Valley reported 6 inches while two National Weather Service employees reported 5 inches in Christoval. Lower elevations near San Angelo reported about 2 to 3 inches of snow. Freezing light rain that fell before the snow caused some limbs to break around Christoval.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Although parts of this six-county North Central Kansas area received a very light dusting of snow on this Wednesday, it managed to avoid the steadier snow and blizzard conditions that slammed parts of Nebraska only 50-100 miles to the north. However, it could not avoid the same feisty northwest winds that its northern neighbor endured, as much of the day featured sustained speeds commonly 30-40 MPH and gusts of 45-60+ MPH. While observations from nearby/surrounding counties strongly suggest that all six local counties observed at least sporadic/brief instances of sustained 40 MPH and/or 58+ MPH gusts, the only verified severe-criteria gusts within the area included 61 MPH at the Phillipsburg airport and 58 MPH at Rooks County Regional Airport. There were no known ground-truth damage reports. ||In the mid-upper levels, the main driving force behind this high wind event was the passage of a deep, slightly-positively-tilted trough, with its primary vorticity maximum tracking from the Central Rockies on the evening of the 22nd, and then across the heart of Kansas-Nebraska during the day on the 23rd before departing into the Upper Midwest/Upper Great Lakes through the evening-overnight. At the surface, the associated low pressure center gradually intensified from around 994 millibars as it crossed North Central Kansas during the overnight-early morning of the 22nd-23rd, to 988 millibars by mid-day in the IA-MN-WI border area, and then maintained intensity while reaching Lake Superior overnight. Locally, the initial surge of strong northwest winds passed through between midnight-3 a.m. behind the main synoptic cold front, but gusts largely peaked around 50 MPH or less. The overall-strongest winds of the day then occurred several hours later between mid-morning and early-afternoon, corresponding to the peak surface pressure gradient between the departing/deepening low and strong high pressure nosing in from the west-northwest (for much of the day the west-to-east gradient across the state of Kansas averaged 12-15 millibars). Between 5-7 p.m. wind gusts diminished to around 30 MPH or less, and they further decreased through the remainder of the night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Periodic gusts near 60 MPH and sustained speeds near 40 MPH occurred across the county. The peak gust of the day was 61 MPH, which was recorded at 9:53 AM and 12:53 PM by the Phillipsburg Airport AWOS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of December 27th, two large bands of snow developed in Colorado and moved into northwest Kansas. The northern most band formed over northeast Colorado and gradually moved south and east along the Kansas-Nebraska-Colorado border. The second band formed over southeast Colorado and slowly moved north into Greeley and Wichita counties before eventually merging with the northern band. Throughout the multi-day event, numerous small bands developed and moved across northwest Kansas producing snow that ranged in depth from a trace to 6 inches, with amounts increasing from south to north across the area. Light freezing drizzle produced a glaze of ice in Logan County. The highest snowfall totals occurred in northwest Sheridan County. Injuries were reported with accidents in Wichita, Logan, and Gove counties. Multiple non-injury accidents also occurred across Thomas, Logan, and Gove counties. Numerous vehicle slide-offs were also reported across Sherman, Thomas, and Cheyenne counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple snow bands moved across Wichita county, producing only a trace of snow. While snow accumulations were low, roads became slick. At 8:07 am CST on December 29th, a passenger vehicle accident was reported on KS-25 near mile marker 118. One person was injured. Key impacts: traffic accident.

At 7:49 pm CST on December 28th, a rollover accident occurred on US-40 between County Roads 360 and 370 with a passenger vehicle containing five passengers. Three injuries were reported. At 11:36 pm CST on December 28th, a 2 passenger vehicle collision occurred on I-70 near mile marker 79. No injuries were reported with the second accident. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The northwestern portion of Kansas saw non-thunderstorm high sustained winds and gusts associated with a cold front beginning in the afternoon hours of December 22nd that continued until the afternoon hours of December 23rd. The Goodland, KS ASOS recorded both the highest sustained winds at 46 mph and the highest wind gust at 66 mph. These winds caused damage to property as well as reduced visibilities in the area due to blowing dust and blowing snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Blowing snow caused by high winds was observed via Kansas Department of Highways camera during the afternoon of 12/23/20. The blowing snow reduced visibility down to an estimated 1/4 of a mile. Key impacts: hazardous traveling conditions, blowing snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The active pattern continued to bring cold fronts through the region in late December, and rainfall continued to be confined to the coastal areas and offshore, leaving much of Deep South Texas in a continued dry pattern. These conditions led to the expansion of Extreme (D3) Drought Conditions across nearly all of Zapata County, and maintained the western half of Starr County. Severe (D2) Drought conditions expanded into southeastern Hidalgo County and western Cameron County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: With little to no rainfall across the Rio Grande Plains through the end of December, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to include the majority of Zapata County, while a sliver along the eastern border remained in Severe (D2) Drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system brought high winds and heavy snow to parts of East Tennessee. The storm began with rain and mountain wave high winds during the early morning hours of 12/24. In the afternoon, cold air rapidly swept into the area, changing rain to snow. Moderate to heavy snow fell for about 3-4 hours that evening, resulting in several inches of accumulation. Parts of the central and northern Valley reported between 4 and 7 inches of snow, with up to 12 inches reported in the Smoky Mountains. Scattered to numerous snow showers continued into Christmas Day, with only light additional accumulations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gust was measured by the NOAA/ATDD wind tower at Camp Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of December 27th, two large bands of snow developed in Colorado and moved into northwest Kansas. The northern most band formed over northeast Colorado and gradually moved south and east along the Kansas-Nebraska-Colorado border. The second band formed over southeast Colorado and slowly moved north into Greeley and Wichita counties before eventually merging with the northern band. Throughout the multi-day event, numerous small bands developed and moved across northwest Kansas producing snow that ranged in depth from a trace to 6 inches, with amounts increasing from south to north across the area. Light freezing drizzle produced a glaze of ice in Logan County. The highest snowfall totals occurred in northwest Sheridan County. Injuries were reported with accidents in Wichita, Logan, and Gove counties. Multiple non-injury accidents also occurred across Thomas, Logan, and Gove counties. Numerous vehicle slide-offs were also reported across Sherman, Thomas, and Cheyenne counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple bands of snow moved across Gove County producing a range of snow amounts from a trace to 2 inches. Numerous slide-offs were reported on I-70 and KS-212. At 5:28 pm CST on December 28th, a rollover accident involving a passenger vehicle occurred near mile marker 99 on I-70. No injuries were reported. At 6:05 pm CST on December 28th, a two semi-truck collision occurred resulting in one injury and a truck stuck in a ditch. The accident occurred near mile marker 99 on I-70. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple bands of snow moved northeast across northwest Kansas producing snow ranging in amount from a trace to 2 inches. Two no-injury accidents were reported in Sherman County near the Kansas-Colorado state line the morning of the 11th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow accumulated across Sherman County ranging in amounts from 1 to 2 inches. Two accidents with no injuries occurred near the Colorado-Kansas state line on I-70 around 6:15 am MST. The first accident was a rollover van. The second accident was a semi-truck that jack-knifed into a ditch. A passenger vehicle spin-out also occurred on I-70 near mile marker 31 around 6:20 am MST due to slick roads. No injuries were reported. Key impacts: traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very active weather pattern occurred across the area during the afternoon and lasted overnight as a couple of pre-frontal troughs pivoted across the local bringing a couple rounds of severe storms as the surface low pressure center tracked over the mid-Mississippi Valley during the morning then over the Tennessee Valley into the afternoon. Phased upper level dynamics, an unseasonally moisture airmass, high shear including 0-6 km shear of 60-70 and 0-1 km shear of 20-30, high instability of 500-2000 J/kg surface CAPEs and steep mid level lapse rates near 7 deg C/km all supported a variety of weather threats as these prefrontal troughs moved across the local area. During the afternoon, a pre-frontal cluster of storms raced across SE GA with a very long lived supercell producing multiple tornadoes from across SW GA including Adel to a local touchdown near northern Clinch county near Cogdell then onward to Waycross. This same supercell continued to track NE toward Glynn county and the cities of Hortense and Sterling where it produced very strong downburst damage. During the evening hours, an outflow boundary from the earlier GA storms stalled across NE FL south of the I-10 corridor. The more unstable airmass was south of this boundary as yet another round of severe storms approached from the FL panhandle with a QLCS structure. These storms produced wind damage across NE FL as they tracked across the area through the evening and early morning hours through 4/24.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large oak tree was blown down onto a parsonage that caused roof damage. The portion of the church roof was missing with the siding torn off. Several large cedar trees were snapped nearby. The of the event was based on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During December, portions of three of the six North Central Kansas counties remained in Severe Drought (D2)-or-worse per weekly issuances of the U.S. Drought Monitor, as overall there was very little change to local drought categories during the month despite prevailing below normal precipitation (not unusual for a winter month outside the growing season). More specifically, D2 remained intact across much of northern Phillips and Smith counties along with far northwestern Jewell County, while Extreme Drought (D3) lingered within the extreme northwest edge of Phillips County. Outside of the D2/D3 areas, the remainder of the six-county area was a varied mix of Moderate Drought (D1) and Abnormally Dry (D0), as portions of Jewell, Mitchell, eastern Osborne and southeastern Smith counties actually improved to D0 early in the month (effectively reverting back to what was assigned there in late-October). ||Going into more detail regarding December precipitation trends, it was a fairly dry month across North Central Kansas, marking the fourth month out of the last five to feature prevailing below normal precipitation across most of the area (November being the only somewhat-wetter exception in some spots). The majority of NWS cooperative observer/CoCoRaHS stations only reported between 0.15-0.40 for the month (or generally 25-50 percent of normal). Measured extremes ranged from as much as 0.49 ten miles south-southwest of Beloit and 0.46 in Beloit, to as little as 0.09 near Damar and 0.12 in Smith Center. More significantly, and from a longer-duration perspective covering the five-month-stretch from August-December, a few of the very-driest NWS observer precipitation totals within/near the D3/D2 area included 2.02 at Logan (driest on record), 2.07 at Phillipsburg (driest on record) and 2.71 in Smith Center (2nd-driest on record). Temperature-wise, although certainly not as big of a drought-factor as it would have been during the growing season, December was the second-straight warmer-than-average month, with most local stations averaging 5-6 degrees F above normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northern California typically experiences a wet season, October through May, and a dry season May through September. Strong frontogenesis led to a band of heavy snow on the leading edge of the system on the morning of the 29th. Snow rates exceeded 1+ inches per hour at times through the afternoon and early evening before tapering off later that night.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: While the Hebbronville airport only reported a minimum temperature of 34 degrees, several surrounding observation sites reported lows in the middle to upper 20s. Given the reported low temperatures at the Rancho Los Comitas site in Starr County (28 degrees), the Zapata Airport (26 degrees), as well as the Calosa 1 Mesonet site in Brooks County (29 degrees), it is implied that central and southern Jim Hogg county also saw temperatures fall below freezing. The estimated timing of freezing temperatures is 1:30 AM to 8:30 AM.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough ejected east out of the base of a longwave western US trough, lifting across the southern plains and into Iowa. Strong frontogenesis led to a band of heavy snow on the leading edge of the system on the morning of the 29th. A secondary surge of moisture lifted into the area later in the day thanks to a strong 70 knot low level jet. Precipitation began initially as sleet and freezing rain across southern Iowa with a deep warm inversion above the surface, but by midday precipitation transitioned over to all snow. Snow rates exceeded 1+ inches per hour at times through the afternoon and early evening before tapering off later that night.

A strong storm system brought high winds and heavy snow to parts of East Tennessee. The storm began with rain and mountain wave high winds during the early morning hours of 12/24. In the afternoon, cold air rapidly swept into the area, changing rain to snow. Moderate to heavy snow fell for about 3-4 hours that evening, resulting in several inches of accumulation. Parts of the central and northern Valley reported between 4 and 7 inches of snow, with up to 12 inches reported in the Smoky Mountains. Scattered to numerous snow showers continued into Christmas Day, with only light additional accumulations.

Hurricane Eta originated from a tropical depression that formed in the central Caribbean Sea on October 31st. The depression strengthened into Tropical Storm Eta later that day and continued rapid intensification to major hurricane status on November 2nd while moving westward across the western Caribbean, reaching peak intensity of 150 mph and 923 mb on November 3rd, before making landfall near Puerto Cabezas, Nicaragua. Eta meandered across Nicaragua and Honduras while weakening to a tropical depression through November 5th before emerging over the northwest Caribbean Sea while gradually turning northeast. Eta regained tropical storm status on November 6th and made landfall in Cuba on the 7th, emerged in the Florida Straits and turned westward on the 8th before making landfall in the Florida Keys later that day. The storm made a southwest jog into the southeastern Gulf of Mexico on the 9th before it briefly stalled then turned northward on the 10th. Eta accelerated north-northeast across the eastern Gulf toward the western Florida coast and briefly strengthened to a minimal hurricane during the early morning hours on the 11th, reaching a second peak of 75 mph and 983 mb while centered about 170 miles south-southwest of Tampa. The first landfall was in Puerto Cabezas, Nicaragua before re emerging and making landfall in Cuba and the Florida Keys. Eta made its final landfall in the early morning hours on Nov 12th in Cedar Key with maximum wind speeds of 50 mph and a pressure of 996mb. ASOS site located at the St. Petersburg Airport (KPIE) reported a wind gust of 39 mph/34 kts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level longwave trough emerged out of the Intermountain West and into the Central and Southern Plains during the daytime and evening hours of January 10th. A strong southerly return flow commenced out ahead of the trough during the 8th-9th, allowing for unseasonably warm and humid conditions to advance northward across Southern Oklahoma, much of Central and Eastern Texas, as well as Louisiana, Arkansas, and the Lower Mississippi Valley. Meanwhile, an intensifying surface low pressure system and associated dry line developed along the Red River of North Texas into Southern Oklahoma during the afternoon hours, which spread east northeast across the Ark-La-Tex during the early morning hours on January 11th. With afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 70s ahead of this trough, moderate instability developed across the broad warm sector, with very strong wind shear in place as large scale forcing increased ahead of the trough axis across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. Thus, an axis of strong to severe showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours across Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas and East Texas, which advanced east into North Louisiana during the early morning hours of the 11th. Widespread damaging winds downed trees and power lines across much of Northwest and Northcentral Louisiana, with even a long track tornado developing along the line of severe thunderstorms across Central Bossier, Southern Webster, and Southern Claiborne Parishes. Another isolated tornado touched down in Western Union Parish, before these storms exited the region shortly before daybreak on the 11th. Unfortunately, these storms resulted in four fatalities  across Northwest Louisiana, three of which occurred from the Haughton tornado.

Eta made its final landfall in the early morning hours on Nov 12th in Cedar Key with maximum wind speeds of 50 mph and a pressure of 996mb. An AWOS site located at the Sebring Regional Airport reported a wind gust of 39mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level longwave trough emerged out of the Intermountain West and into the Central and Southern Plains during the daytime and evening hours of January 10th. A strong southerly return flow commenced out ahead of the trough during the 8th-9th, allowing for unseasonably warm and humid conditions to advance northward across Southern Oklahoma, much of Central and Eastern Texas, as well as Louisiana, Arkansas, and the Lower Mississippi Valley. Meanwhile, an intensifying surface low pressure system and associated dry line developed along the Red River of North Texas into Southern Oklahoma during the afternoon hours, which spread east northeast across the Ark-La-Tex during the early morning hours on January 11th. With afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 70s ahead of this trough, moderate instability developed across the broad warm sector, with very strong wind shear in place as large scale forcing increased ahead of the trough axis across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. Thus, an axis of strong to severe showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours across Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas and East Texas, which advanced east into North Louisiana during the early morning hours of the 11th. Damaging winds downed trees and power lines across portions of East Texas, with even multiple tornadoes touching down along the line of severe thunderstorms. Unfortunately, a man  was killed when a tornado touched down west of Nacogdoches and a tree fell on his mobile home. These storms also produced locally heavy rainfall, with amounts of one to three inches, with isolated higher amounts up to four inches recorded across much of this area, resulting in isolated instances of flash flooding. These storms continued to intensify during the late evening and early morning hours as they moved into extreme Eastern Texas and Western Louisiana, producing more in the way of widespread wind damage and isolated tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down in Lindale.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long track 40+ mile long EF-2 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 135 mph first touched down just south of Barksdale Air Force Base off of Sligo Road in Central Bossier Parish, where it snapped and uprooted hundreds of softwood and hardwood trees and damaged several carports and outbuildings. The tornado then crossed the far southeast corner of Barksdale Air Force Base where at least one hundred trees were snapped or uprooted. After the tornado exited the corner of Barksdale Air Force Base, it strengthened south of Haughton to produce its most significant damage, completely destroying a single-wide manufactured home and a double-wide manufactured home off of Davis Road. Two fatalities (a 79 year old male and his 65 year old wife) occurred in the double-wide with an additional fatality (an 87 year old male) occurring in the single-wide. The tornado continued to produce roof damage and uproot and snap trees which fell into homes in Eastern Bossier Parish, concentrated most along James Lane. The tornado continued moving northeast across Oliver Road and Camp Zion Road, where numerous trees were snapped and uprooted, while also removing siding off of a single-wide manufactured home, and ripping a portion of the metal exterior and doors off of the Bossier Parish Fire District 1 Station 6 building, as well as tearing off some vinyl siding to a mobile home living quarters located next door, before crossing over into Webster Parish.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An excessive heat event occurred over the Labor Day weekend as afternoon temperatures climbed upwards of 115-120 degrees across the area. In Joshua Tree National Park, two individuals set out on a hike around noon on the 5th in the Turkey Flats area. One of the hikers, a 20 year old male, became unconscious and the other called authorities for immediate aid at 1900PDT. Park authorities located the hikers around 2330PDT and administered CPR to the unconscious hiker, but were unable to revive him. The hiker was later pronounced dead at around 0900PDT on the 6th with the cause of death being heat-caused.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Eta originated from a tropical depression that formed in the central Caribbean Sea on October 31st. Eta meandered across Nicaragua and Honduras while weakening to a tropical depression through November 5th before emerging over the northwest Caribbean Sea while gradually turning northeast. Eta regained tropical storm status on November 6th and made landfall in Cuba on the 7th, emerged in the Florida Straits and turned westward on the 8th before making landfall in the Florida Keys later that day. The storm made a southwest jog into the southeastern Gulf of Mexico on the 9th before it briefly stalled then turned northward on the 10th. Eta accelerated north-northeast across the eastern Gulf toward the western Florida coast and briefly strengthened to a minimal hurricane during the early morning hours on the 11th, reaching a second peak of 75 mph and 983 mb while centered about 170 miles south-southwest of Tampa. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level longwave trough emerged out of the Intermountain West and into the Central and Southern Plains during the daytime and evening hours of January 10th. A strong southerly return flow commenced out ahead of the trough during the 8th-9th, allowing for unseasonably warm and humid conditions to advance northward across Southern Oklahoma, much of Central and Eastern Texas, as well as Louisiana, Arkansas, and the Lower Mississippi Valley. Meanwhile, an intensifying surface low pressure system and associated dry line developed along the Red River of North Texas into Southern Oklahoma during the afternoon hours, which spread east northeast across the Ark-La-Tex during the early morning hours on January 11th. With afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 70s ahead of this trough, moderate instability developed across the broad warm sector, with very strong wind shear in place as large scale forcing increased ahead of the trough axis across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. Thus, an axis of strong to severe showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours across Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas and East Texas, which advanced east into North Louisiana during the early morning hours of the 11th. Widespread damaging winds downed trees and power lines across much of Northwest and Northcentral Louisiana, with even a long track tornado developing along the line of severe thunderstorms across Central Bossier, Southern Webster, and Southern Claiborne Parishes. Another isolated tornado touched down in Western Union Parish, before these storms exited the region shortly before daybreak on the 11th. Unfortunately, these storms resulted in four fatalities  across Northwest Louisiana, three of which occurred from the Haughton tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level longwave trough emerged out of the Intermountain West and into the Central and Southern Plains during the daytime and evening hours of January 10th. A strong southerly return flow commenced out ahead of the trough during the 8th-9th, allowing for unseasonably warm and humid conditions to advance northward across Southern Oklahoma, much of Central and Eastern Texas, as well as Louisiana, Arkansas, and the Lower Mississippi Valley. Meanwhile, an intensifying surface low pressure system and associated dry line developed along the Red River of North Texas into Southern Oklahoma during the afternoon hours, which spread east northeast across the Ark-La-Tex during the early morning hours on January 11th. With afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 70s ahead of this trough, moderate instability developed across the broad warm sector, with very strong wind shear in place as large scale forcing increased ahead of the trough axis across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. Thus, an axis of strong to severe showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours across Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas and East Texas, which advanced east into North Louisiana during the early morning hours of the 11th. Damaging winds downed trees and power lines across portions of East Texas, with even multiple tornadoes touching down along the line of severe thunderstorms. Unfortunately, a man  was killed when a tornado touched down west of Nacogdoches and a tree fell on his mobile home. These storms also produced locally heavy rainfall, with amounts of one to three inches, with isolated higher amounts up to four inches recorded across much of this area, resulting in isolated instances of flash flooding. These storms continued to intensify during the late evening and early morning hours as they moved into extreme Eastern Texas and Western Louisiana, producing more in the way of widespread wind damage and isolated tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 110 mph touched down along Highway 84 near the intersection of County Road 4234 west of Mount Enterprise, snapping and uprooting a few trees. The tornado continued eastward roughly along Highway 84, intensifying and snapping numerous trees in the Reagan Branch bottom, just west of the Farm to Market Road 225 intersection. It continued east-northeast snapping and uprooting trees as it crossed County Roads 3223, 3226, and 3206. Several farm outbuildings were tossed and completely destroyed along County Road 3206, with two residences sustaining roof damage, before the tornado lifted just northeast of the intersection of County Road 3206 and 3166.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms tracked across much of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois in the early afternoon hours of May 23rd, 2020. Seven tornadoes were confirmed from this event in Iowa and Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A  tornado developed ENE of Morrison, IL in Whiteside County, shortly before 2:30 pm. The tornado was on the ground for about 24 minutes along an intermittent 12 mile path.

Buildings had uplift and removal of roof decking, outer walls collapsed. Two buildings were destroyed and five had major|damage. Several buildings in a boat storage facility had major damage and large 2-ton boats where thrown about. The damage became more spotty as it approached U.S. Highway 19. The tornado then weakened and lifted as it reached the eastern edge of the Howard Franklin Bridge with no further damage observed. In total, 4 warehouses were destroyed with 9 receiving major damage and 6 others receiving minor damage. 1 home received major damage and 17 others received minor damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level longwave trough emerged out of the Intermountain West and into the Central and Southern Plains during the daytime and evening hours of January 10th. A strong southerly return flow commenced out ahead of the trough during the 8th-9th, allowing for unseasonably warm and humid conditions to advance northward across Southern Oklahoma, much of Central and Eastern Texas, as well as Louisiana, Arkansas, and the Lower Mississippi Valley. Meanwhile, an intensifying surface low pressure system and associated dry line developed along the Red River of North Texas into Southern Oklahoma during the afternoon hours, which spread east northeast across the Ark-La-Tex during the early morning hours on January 11th. With afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 70s ahead of this trough, moderate instability developed across the broad warm sector, with very strong wind shear in place as large scale forcing increased ahead of the trough axis across East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. Thus, an axis of strong to severe showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours across Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas and East Texas, which advanced east into North Louisiana during the early morning hours of the 11th. Widespread damaging winds downed trees and power lines across much of Northwest and Northcentral Louisiana, with even a long track tornado developing along the line of severe thunderstorms across Central Bossier, Southern Webster, and Southern Claiborne Parishes. Another isolated tornado touched down in Western Union Parish, before these storms exited the region shortly before daybreak on the 11th. Unfortunately, these storms resulted in four fatalities  across Northwest Louisiana, three of which occurred from the Haughton tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 107 mph touched down on the east side of Highway 550 between Milton and Mariola Road. Here, it uprooted and snapped softwood trees, before continuing northeast in the embedded squall line which was also doing wind damage along both sides of the main tornado path. The most significant tornado damage occurred along Clayton Foster and Christine Roads, where it completely tore off the metal roofs from two chicken houses, and snapped and uprooted several hardwood and softwood trees. Additional chicken house damage occurred on the south end of the tornado closer to Christine Road, where a portion of the tin roof was peeled back, and metal roofing was thrown hundreds of feet along the main tornado path. The tornado finished its life cycle along Thomas Wade Road, where it ripped more metal roofing from chicken houses, and tossed them in a southerly direction away from the main circulation. The tornado lifted at this location, although areas near and east of Highway 15 continued to experience straight line wind damage along the path of the squall line as it moved across Central Union Parish.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning hours on October 26th, a strong cold front dropped south through far southeast California and in the process, strong and gusty northerly winds developed across portions of eastern Riverside County. Some of the strongest winds occurred to the south of Joshua Tree National Park between Indio and Desert Center. Around 0500 PDT, north winds estimated to be at least 40 mph sustained blew over several semi tractor-trailer trucks driving on Interstate 10. A High Wind Warning was in effect at the time the trucks were blown over. There were no injuries reported to the drivers of the trucks.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Following a cold frontal passage, strong gusty north winds developed to the south of Joshua Tree National Park and in the vicinity of Chiriaco Summitt. Sustained winds of at least 40 mph developed and according to the department of highways, they blew over two semi-trucks driving on Interstate 10 about 3 miles west of Chiriaco Summit. It was likely that there were even stronger gusts at the time the trucks were blown over. High profile vehicles such as semis are extremely vulnerable to north winds that blow perpendicular to the interstate. There were no reports of injuries to the drivers. A High Wind Warning was in effect at the time of the accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry conditions and anomalously low fuel moisture, in combination with an unstable low-to-mid-level atmosphere, allowed the Loyalton wildfire to develop extreme fire behavior on the afternoon of 15 August 2020. Robust heat and moisture fluxes from the wildfire caused rapid smoke plume deepening and lofting of pyrometeors above the lifting condensation level, which led to the formation of two vertically extensive pyrocumulonimbi and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesoanticyclone embedded within a deep pyrocumulonimbus updraft inside the Loyalton wildfire perimeter generated an EF1 rated anticyclonic tornado that snapped (DI 28, DOD 4) and uprooted (DI 28, DOD 3) several Jeffrey pine trees along a 0.43-mile path within Roberts Canyon. The tornado spun up 0.15 miles north-northeast of the intersection of Forest Service Road 182 and Forest Service Road 31182 and dissipated 0.44 miles east of the aforementioned intersection. The damage path had a maximum width of 137 yards. No injuries or deaths occurred with this tornado.

Dry conditions and anomalously low fuel moisture, in combination with an unstable low-to-mid-level atmosphere, allowed the Loyalton wildfire to develop extreme fire behavior on the afternoon of 15 August 2020. Robust heat and moisture fluxes from the wildfire caused rapid smoke plume deepening and lofting of pyrometeors above the lifting condensation level, which led to the formation of two vertically extensive pyrocumulonimbi and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bystanders along CA 70 and US 395 near Hallelujah Junction captured multiple videos and photographs of an anticyclonically rotating tornado pendant to the base of a pyrocumulonimbus cloud. The tornado caused no damage from which the NWS could assign an EF-scale rating as it traversed across an area of burned sagebrush. From photographs and video evidence, the approximate path of the tornado was calculated. The tornado traveled along a 3.16-mile path from the head of Roberts Canyon to 1.33 miles southwest of Hallelujah Junction. The maximum path width was approximately 156 yards. No injuries or deaths occurred with this tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front stalled across the Minnesota and Iowa border for a few days finally made a push across the state, providing a focus for convective development. Deep layer shear of 30 to 40 knots and CAPE over 2000 J/kg were sufficient for storm development. As the line of storms moved across the state with the front, several hail cores developed resulting in quarter sized hail in east central Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported mostly dime sized hail with a few stones up to quarter sized, accompanied by estimated 40 mph winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak shortwave moved across the state, and while CAPE values were bewteen 2000-3000 J/kg limited deep layer shear made it difficult for any significant convection to develop. Isolated storms developed across northern Iowa in the early evening, however they were unable to strengthen to severe limits. With steep low level lapse rates and sufficient low level shear, storms did manage to develop two funnel clouds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of a funnel cloud west of Pocahontas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Minimal rainfall during the summer led to the continued deterioration of conditions across portions of west central into central Iowa.  Extreme drought conditions developed in early August and remained for the rest of the month as little rainfall occurred.  August ended up being the 3rd driest on record across Iowa with slightly above normal temperatures.  Along with maturation of field crops, soil moisture became very low with small streams drying up by the end of the month in many locations in the extreme area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Very dry conditions since late spring and the continuation of these conditions in August led to the expansion of severe to extreme drought conditions in Greene county during the month.

Basic Summary: A cluster of storms in northeast Nebraska and southeast South Dakota developed into the destructive derecho that raced eastward across large portions of Iowa, northern Illinois, southern Wisconsin, northern Indiana, and southern Michigan during the morning and afternoon of August 10th. The strongest winds were experienced in central and east-central Iowa where 100+ mph winds were observed. Some of the strongest winds were in an area from roughly Marshalltown, IA eastward along the Highway 30 corridor to the Mississippi River, where estimated winds exceeded 120+ mph and approached 140 mph. A number of QLCS tornadoes were also experienced within the Highway 30 corridor. One of the most remarkable aspects of the derecho was the duration of severe winds, with many areas experiencing at least periodic, if not persistent, severe level (58+ mph) winds over a roughly 30 minute time frame. As the derecho moved eastward out of Iowa, it continued to expand, but weakened from its peak strength. Winds continued to exceed severe criteria (58+ mph) in Illinois, Wisconsin, Indiana, and Michigan and began to produce additional QLCS tornadoes across northern Illinois before fading out across northern Indiana and southern Michigan.||In the wake of the derecho, damage was substantial in many areas, rural and urban. Many agriculture fields, mainly corn, were flattened within the swaths of strongest winds. Initial estimates suggest at least 850,000 acres of partial or complete crop loss occurred from this event. Within urban and wooded areas extensive tree and structure damage was seen, including complete roof failure in a few instances. At its peak, total estimated customers without power exceeded 1.4 million across the affected states. In total, early estimates on losses (agriculture, infrastructure, private property) have exceeded $7.5 billion across the states affected. ||Environment: Broadly speaking, it was a ripe day for thunderstorms across the affected area with MUCAPE values often exceeding 3500-4000 J/kg by the mid morning hours concurrent with mid-upper level short wave support, and indications that any cold pool development would be strong (difference between cold pool and ambient air) and potentially long lived. For detailed environmental analysis, including soundings, please view the various local NWS office event review pages: NWS Des Moines, NWS Quad Cities, NWS Chicago, NWS Milwaukee, NWS Central Illinois, NWS Northern Indiana, or NWS Indianapolis.||Additional Details: Numerous injuries occurred during the derecho and in the aftermath during cleanup, including 4 direct and indirect deaths of which 3 occurred in Iowa (two in Poweshiek County and one in Linn County) and 1 in Indiana (Fort Wayne).||Disclaimer: The August 10, 2020 derecho resulted in widespread high-end damage across large portions of central and southern Iowa. Given the size and scope of the event and understanding that final damage and loss estimates (agriculture, infrastructure, and private property) will take months to complete, the NWS is not able to estimate the monetary impact at this time. Values may be added as more data becomes from various sources in future months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported a large tree limb 6 inches in diameter and 20 feet long was downed. Several smaller limbs were downed as well.

Some of the strongest winds were in an area from roughly Marshalltown, IA eastward along the Highway 30 corridor to the Mississippi River, where estimated winds exceeded 120+ mph and approached 140 mph. A number of QLCS tornadoes were also experienced within the Highway 30 corridor. One of the most remarkable aspects of the derecho was the duration of severe winds, with many areas experiencing at least periodic, if not persistent, severe level (58+ mph) winds over a roughly 30 minute time frame. As the derecho moved eastward out of Iowa, it continued to expand, but weakened from its peak strength. Winds continued to exceed severe criteria (58+ mph) in Illinois, Wisconsin, Indiana, and Michigan and began to produce additional QLCS tornadoes across northern Illinois before fading out across northern Indiana and southern Michigan.||In the wake of the derecho, damage was substantial in many areas, rural and urban. Many agriculture fields, mainly corn, were flattened within the swaths of strongest winds. Initial estimates suggest at least 850,000 acres of partial or complete crop loss occurred from this event. Within urban and wooded areas extensive tree and structure damage was seen, including complete roof failure in a few instances. At its peak, total estimated customers without power exceeded 1.4 million across the affected states. In total, early estimates on losses (agriculture, infrastructure, private property) have exceeded $7.5 billion across the states affected. ||Environment: Broadly speaking, it was a ripe day for thunderstorms across the affected area with MUCAPE values often exceeding 3500-4000 J/kg by the mid morning hours concurrent with mid-upper level short wave support, and indications that any cold pool development would be strong (difference between cold pool and ambient air) and potentially long lived. For detailed environmental analysis, including soundings, please view the various local NWS office event review pages: NWS Des Moines, NWS Quad Cities, NWS Chicago, NWS Milwaukee, NWS Central Illinois, NWS Northern Indiana, or NWS Indianapolis.||Additional Details: Numerous injuries occurred during the derecho and in the aftermath during cleanup, including 4 direct and indirect deaths of which 3 occurred in Iowa (two in Poweshiek County and one in Linn County) and 1 in Indiana (Fort Wayne).||Disclaimer: The August 10, 2020 derecho resulted in widespread high-end damage across large portions of central and southern Iowa. Given the size and scope of the event and understanding that final damage and loss estimates (agriculture, infrastructure, and private property) will take months to complete, the NWS is not able to estimate the monetary impact at this time. Values may be added as more data becomes from various sources in future months.

Some of the strongest winds were in an area from roughly Marshalltown, IA eastward along the Highway 30 corridor to the Mississippi River, where estimated winds exceeded 120+ mph and approached 140 mph. A number of QLCS tornadoes were also experienced within the Highway 30 corridor. One of the most remarkable aspects of the derecho was the duration of severe winds, with many areas experiencing at least periodic, if not persistent, severe level (58+ mph) winds over a roughly 30 minute time frame. As the derecho moved eastward out of Iowa, it continued to expand, but weakened from its peak strength. Winds continued to exceed severe criteria (58+ mph) in Illinois, Wisconsin, Indiana, and Michigan and began to produce additional QLCS tornadoes across northern Illinois before fading out across northern Indiana and southern Michigan.||In the wake of the derecho, damage was substantial in many areas, rural and urban. Many agriculture fields, mainly corn, were flattened within the swaths of strongest winds. Initial estimates suggest at least 850,000 acres of partial or complete crop loss occurred from this event. Within urban and wooded areas extensive tree and structure damage was seen, including complete roof failure in a few instances. At its peak, total estimated customers without power exceeded 1.4 million across the affected states. In total, early estimates on losses (agriculture, infrastructure, private property) have exceeded $7.5 billion across the states affected. ||Environment: Broadly speaking, it was a ripe day for thunderstorms across the affected area with MUCAPE values often exceeding 3500-4000 J/kg by the mid morning hours concurrent with mid-upper level short wave support, and indications that any cold pool development would be strong (difference between cold pool and ambient air) and potentially long lived. For detailed environmental analysis, including soundings, please view the various local NWS office event review pages: NWS Des Moines, NWS Quad Cities, NWS Chicago, NWS Milwaukee, NWS Central Illinois, NWS Northern Indiana, or NWS Indianapolis.||Additional Details: Numerous injuries occurred during the derecho and in the aftermath during cleanup, including 4 direct and indirect deaths of which 3 occurred in Iowa (two in Poweshiek County and one in Linn County) and 1 in Indiana (Fort Wayne).||Disclaimer: The August 10, 2020 derecho resulted in widespread high-end damage across large portions of central and southern Iowa. Given the size and scope of the event and understanding that final damage and loss estimates (agriculture, infrastructure, and private property) will take months to complete, the NWS is not able to estimate the monetary impact at this time. Values may be added as more data becomes from various sources in future months.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Very dry conditions since late spring and the continuation of these conditions in August led to the expansion of severe to extreme drought conditions in Calhoun county during the month.

Some of the strongest winds were in an area from roughly Marshalltown, IA eastward along the Highway 30 corridor to the Mississippi River, where estimated winds exceeded 120+ mph and approached 140 mph. A number of QLCS tornadoes were also experienced within the Highway 30 corridor. One of the most remarkable aspects of the derecho was the duration of severe winds, with many areas experiencing at least periodic, if not persistent, severe level (58+ mph) winds over a roughly 30 minute time frame. As the derecho moved eastward out of Iowa, it continued to expand, but weakened from its peak strength. Winds continued to exceed severe criteria (58+ mph) in Illinois, Wisconsin, Indiana, and Michigan and began to produce additional QLCS tornadoes across northern Illinois before fading out across northern Indiana and southern Michigan.||In the wake of the derecho, damage was substantial in many areas, rural and urban. Many agriculture fields, mainly corn, were flattened within the swaths of strongest winds. Initial estimates suggest at least 850,000 acres of partial or complete crop loss occurred from this event. Within urban and wooded areas extensive tree and structure damage was seen, including complete roof failure in a few instances. At its peak, total estimated customers without power exceeded 1.4 million across the affected states. In total, early estimates on losses (agriculture, infrastructure, private property) have exceeded $7.5 billion across the states affected. ||Environment: Broadly speaking, it was a ripe day for thunderstorms across the affected area with MUCAPE values often exceeding 3500-4000 J/kg by the mid morning hours concurrent with mid-upper level short wave support, and indications that any cold pool development would be strong (difference between cold pool and ambient air) and potentially long lived. For detailed environmental analysis, including soundings, please view the various local NWS office event review pages: NWS Des Moines, NWS Quad Cities, NWS Chicago, NWS Milwaukee, NWS Central Illinois, NWS Northern Indiana, or NWS Indianapolis.||Additional Details: Numerous injuries occurred during the derecho and in the aftermath during cleanup, including 4 direct and indirect deaths of which 3 occurred in Iowa (two in Poweshiek County and one in Linn County) and 1 in Indiana (Fort Wayne).||Disclaimer: The August 10, 2020 derecho resulted in widespread high-end damage across large portions of central and southern Iowa. Given the size and scope of the event and understanding that final damage and loss estimates (agriculture, infrastructure, and private property) will take months to complete, the NWS is not able to estimate the monetary impact at this time. Values may be added as more data becomes from various sources in future months.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late season snow in the early morning of April 15th left a coating of 1 to 2 inches across much of northeast Illinois.  This snow melted on most roadways but accumulated on bridges and overpasses causing them to become icy.  Numerous traffic accidents occurred including a 60 vehicle pile-up on Interstate 90/94 near Division Street in Chicago.  There were 14 people sent to hospitals, though none of their injuries were life threatening.  Another 45 people were treated at the scene.  Various interstates in the Chicago metro area were closed due other accidents and icy bridge conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm developed in the warm sector region south of an approaching, weakening cold front. As high pressure slid east off into the Atlantic Ocean, southeast flow increased, enhancing moisture throughout the column. Daytime heated steepened lapse rates which destabilized the atmosphere. A thunderstorm was able to capitalize on available instability to producing damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed power lines and trees across the Montz area. A mobile home canopy was damaged by thunderstorm wind gusts on Hollywood Park Drive.

In fact, intensifying from tropical depression to Category strength in 40 hours is the fastest rate of intensification of any storm on record in the Atlantic Basin. Delta quickly weakened to a category 1 hurricane after making its first landfall on the Yucatan Peninsula. It gradually recurved north towards the Louisiana coastline, fluctuating in intensity between Category 2 and 3. Hurricane Delta ultimately arrived with an intensity of 105 mph, a strong category 2 storm. Local impacts include 50 to 70 MPH wind gusts across the area, storm surge of 2 to 3 feet above ground and widespread tree and structural damage. There were 6 injuries. In addition, outer bands of Delta produced a significant amount of rainfall on the north side of Baton Rouge Metro. Upwards of 5 to 10 inches of rain fell, causing street flooding in Baton Rouge and moderate river flooding in the region. Delta caused approximately $100 million worth of damage across southeast Louisiana. ||It made landfall around 5 pm east of Cameron LA or about 15 miles east of where Category 4 Hurricane Laura made landfall just a couple of months earlier this year. Delta became the 4th named storm to make landfall in Louisiana this hurricane season.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delta produced minor impacts as a result of tropical storm force winds across the parish. Peak wind gusts were estimated in the 50 to 60 mph range. A few trees were downed and at the peak, roughly 20 percent of the parish was without power.
